#1103. Life as a Wag in the transfer window

"Owen was on the phone to the manager and his agent while I was in labour. They waited for me to give birth and then he went out on loan pretty much as soon as I was out of hospital."

Owen Dale's loan deal wasn't to a local club, but to Portsmouth - a city more than 200 miles away. His partner, Jessica Beaumont, had never even been there.

And the pair had only just got the keys to a house they had bought. They would end up staying in it for just one night.

"Since living together, we've moved five times in five years," says Jessica.

"You have to be prepared for anything in the transfer window. But it's also a really fortunate position to be in at a young age."

This period - when clubs are permitted to buy, sell and loan players - takes place twice a year, in January and during the summer, for clubs in the Premier League, the English Football League (EFL) and the Women's Super League (WSL).

While a select few stay in one place throughout their career, for most players moving from club to club is just part of life in the modern game.

Jessica met Owen when he was at Crewe Alexandra. A move to Blackpool soon followed.

"I didn't get together with him because he was a footballer so I never considered the footballer life - that he might just have to move at the last minute," she says. "We just met and we clicked."

But it soon became apparent that dealing with almost constant uncertainty would be part of that life.

The move to Blackpool was a loan, with an option to buy, so for six months - during which Jessica was pregnant with their son Xavier - they did not know whether he would be staying there or heading back to Crewe.

Blackpool decided to sign Owen, but he was soon out on loan again. This isn't uncommon, with loan deals a way for clubs to help young prospects gain first-team experience and get regular playing time elsewhere.

"When the move to Portsmouth happened it really hit me - I had to quickly realise that 'OK this is now my life'," says Jessica.

Just before Owen's loan deal to Portsmouth the couple had bought their first house together in Congleton - a town close to Jessica's family in Stoke on Trent, and commutable to Blackpool.

"We spent one night in there - we hadn't even unpacked," she says.

They decided a 10-hour round trip on Owen's day off in the week to see his newborn son was not an option.

"We thought 'if he's not playing well because he's tired, what's the point in doing this'?" says Jessica, who adds that they ended up renting out the Congleton house and have been living in rented accommodation themselves ever since.

"I was finishing my law degree and had a job at the time - I had to say to them I wouldn't be coming back from maternity leave," she says.

Post-natal complications also made it difficult for her to travel at the time.

"I had Owen on the phone basically saying, 'I've done a couple of house viewings. I've chosen this one. This is where we're going to be living' and showing me on FaceTime," she recalls.

"In that moment I did feel really out of control."

Uprooting her life at short notice and leaving her family behind was challenging and Jessica remembers spending a lot of time alone in Portsmouth when Owen was at away games.

But she remembers lots of positives from that time too, including when she became friends with another player's partner.

"I was so fortunate that she would often stay with me when Owen was away," she says.

"I say to her all the time that I'll appreciate that time forever because I was just so isolated.

"Our schedules were the same - when Owen went away her partner was also away - I didn't have to be fully alone and she got it."

Owen made 28 appearances for Plymouth Argyle last season

Owen, now 27, has played most of his career in League One, with two stints in the Championship when we was with Blackpool and Oxford United.

Last season was spent on loan at Plymouth Argyle and he is currently a free agent - this means he is not tied to any club by a legal contract. Owen can now join a new team without a transfer fee because no former employer owns his registration rights.

Many of his moves have been on deadline day and he says he is "very aware of the sacrifices" his family make.

"There's always the risk that a move might not work," he says. "So I might uproot my whole family for this next venture and it all goes south.

"Over the years I've learned that until there's a contract signed on the dotted line, you could end up anywhere."

Owen went on loan to Portsmouth in 2022 just days after Jessica gave birth to Xavier

Owen returned to Blackpool the following year and made 32 appearances for the Tangerines

The family moved to Bicester in 2024, as Owen helped Oxford United win promotion to the Championship

Owen joined Wigan Athletic on loan the following year making his debut in a 2â1 FA Cup fourth-round defeat by Fulham

Last season the family lived in Devon after Owen went on loan again - this time to Plymouth Argyle

For now, Jessica's career in law is on hold, she instead has a job in social media and works from home.

She also posts about her experiences on TikTok, regularly using #wag and #waglife.

"My career can be picked up at any time - whereas his career is right now and you've really got to take every opportunity," she says.

"As much as people say it's a glamorous lifestyle you do make sacrifices so your partner can have their dream and get themselves as far as they can in football.

"At the end of the day, as much as I'm involved, it's his career. That means in order for me to support him properly I can't get emotionally involved."

This includes not getting too emotionally attached to where they live.

"We usually rent newer houses that are a blank canvas so we can make them our own, although this last season the accommodation was provided furnished by Argyle," she says.

"We put a lot of Xavier's toys and garden stuff in storage and referred to our Plymouth accommodation as 'the holiday house'.

"It can be hard when he asks us to get things like his trampoline which we don't have with us."

Owen's career is always the priority, Jessica says.

"When Owen was at Oxford he had one year left on his contract and I loved it there," she says.

"But the best thing was for him to go and get game time somewhere miles away. So we moved."

While Premier League footballers can earn tens of thousands of pounds a week - sometimes hundreds of thousands - life in the lower leagues can be very different.

"When you think 'Wag' [players' wives and girlfriends] and you think 'footballer', both of those terms come with this stereotype that our lives are easy," Jessica says.

"People also put League One players in the same bracket as Premier League players.

"In the Premier League they're often set up for life - we can't live in that way because we have to prepare for life after football."

Adding to the uncertainty of where they will be playing is also the possibility or relegation or injury.

"When we were at Portsmouth, Blackpool was still his parent club and they got relegated," says Jessica. "Owen wasn't even involved that season, but his wage was still affected.

"You have to be prepared for everything. You just can't live outside of your means.

"But it's still a really fortunate position to be in.

"Luckily, Owen's been good with injuries. There are some players who they get injured in the last month of the season and they're out of contract.

"In football things can be really positive or really negative."

The uncertainty also affects their children - four-year-old Xavier and two-month old Etta.

"Now that Xavier is growing up - he's fast approaching school age - another thing that will have to be added into the mix is his stability," says Jessica.

Even normal things like organising his recent fourth birthday party aren't always straightforward.

"We couldn't plan to have a party in Plymouth with balloons and cakes etc because we didn't know if we were going to be there," she says.

"Instead we planned a party near my family in Stoke-on-Trent - we needed to make something work regardless of what happens with Owen's job.

"As much as I worry about Xavier and Etta, I also think how amazing it's going to be for them when they're older to be able to tell their life story and say they've lived in all these different places.

"I think it's teaching them a good life lesson that they don't need to be tied to one place."

She says they have made every move a positive experience.

"We've said to Xavier that we might be moving soon and when we do we're going to get his bike back out of storage," says Jessica.

"That way he knows that moving is a possibility and hopefully he's not thinking about what he's going to lose but what he's going to gain.

"The fortunate thing for us is that Xavier loves football. He gets a lot of excitement as well from the new strips and the new chants and all of that kind of thing."

Xavier has enjoyed watching his dad play at each of his new clubs

So, does Jessica have any tips for people in a similar situation?

"The main thing for me personally - and what I've learned first hand - is the importance of keeping your own identity outside of football," she says.

"If you get too wrapped up in it, it only puts more pressure on your partner.

"If you can get a hobby, a routine or even a work-from-home job, that can help - things that can move with you."

Being sensible financially is also important.

"I'd also say that if you have a season where you get promoted, try not to change your lifestyle and to bank the promotion money so that you have as much stability as you can," she adds.

"In our house, I de-clutter maybe once a month," she says. "This helps me because I don't have control over Owen's career. But what I do have control over is making sure that if and when anything does happen, the house is ready to be packed up and moved.

"When it's the transfer window I will plan in one-week blocks - that gives me that little bit of certainty in a situation where I have no control."

She admits "it can be hard" but "on the flip side it's so exciting".

"We've lived in places that we never would have lived in. And that's exciting for a relationship," she adds.

"You know, with some relationships you can get bored.

#1102. 73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it

Harry Kane is one of the leading names in the race for this year's Ballon d'Or, having scored 73 goals last season for club and country

As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.

Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.

When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.

"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.

I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.

Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.

From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.

Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.

The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.

As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.

And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.

Kane's role has evolved drastically over the past nine years, with the striker now heavily involved in all phases of the game -Â including as deep as his own box

"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.

"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."

Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.

Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.

Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.

Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.

After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.

Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.

Kane wins his individual battle with Waldemar Anton, shielding the ball and showcasing strength

As he rises, he positions his body to the right, facing his own goal.

Through clever body positioning, Kane moves the opposition towards the right side of the pitch. This is his cue to cut the ball back into the open space

This allows Kane to evade two defenders, now facing the opposition's goal

Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.

"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?

"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."

In the second minute of Bayern Munich's game against Arsenal, Kane dropped deep into a position normally occupied by centre-backs. Arsenal centre-back William Saliba marked him all the way, vacating space higher up the pitch

There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.

Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.

"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.

"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.

"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."

Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 -Â in a front two.

"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."

Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.

"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.

"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."

Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.

"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."

It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.

"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."

The Frankfurt midfielder notices Kane dropping deep. Recognising this danger, he moves towards him.

With Frankfurt's central midfielder pulled towards Kane, Luis Diaz is able to receive a pass between the lines. He forms a central front two with Kane. The wingers ahead of them, Serge Gnabry and Michael Olise, push the defensive line back.

Kane is found in space around the edge of the box and strikes the ball hard into the net

The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.

Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder -Â something he recognises and exploits.

Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.

"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.

"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.

"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.

"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.

"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back."

Karl receives the ball in the middle of the pitch. As seen in yellow, Kane is being marked by Club Brugge's holding midfielder, rather than any of the central defenders

Kane, recognising this, makes a diagonal run in behind, pulling the opposition holding midfielder away from the centre of the pitch

Karl drives with the ball into the space created by Kane before putting the ball into the top corner

With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.

Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.

He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.

In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

What is the aim for Kompany, Kane and Bayern?

#1101. Arsenal had more than 20 players on shortlist to capitalise on title win

Arsenal had more than 20 players on shortlist to capitalise on title win

Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.

An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.

If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.

The plans were ambitious: a shortlist with more than 20 players on it. They were targets at Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, even at Chelsea and Tottenham.

But as the window shut on Tuesday night, you could not escape the sense of unfulfillment - certainly from a section of supporters.

Arsenal's close season was one characterised by some unquestionable successes, but also riddled by difficulties and frustration.

Ahead of their home match against Chelsea on Sunday, BBC Sport details Arsenal's transfer window and whether manager Mikel Arteta, sporting director Andrea Berta and, perhaps most pertinently, owners Kroenke Sports Entertainment can deem their summer operation a success.

Bruno Guimaraes's Â£75m capture from Newcastle United was Arsenal's most eye-catching signing.

Heading into the summer, Arsenal were keeping abreast of Guimaraes' situation at Newcastle, although others were considered a higher priority.

For instance, their interest in Elliot Anderson was widely reported, but it was clear the England international was joining Manchester City.

Guimaraes' former Newcastle team-mate Sandro Tonali and Bournemouth's Alex Scott were also among the midfielders explored before a move for the South American accelerated.

At the ages of 26 and 23 respectively, Tonali and Scott are younger than Guimaraes, who turns 29 in November.

But numerous factors, including availability and price - Tonali joined Spurs for a minimum Â£92m - made their signings difficult.

Aston Villa's Amadou Onana was also among the options considered, but the Belgium international suffered a serious knee injury at the World Cup.

By mid-June Guimaraes, who had universal backing inside the Emirates, emerged as the club's primary focus.

Berta knew the player's camp well and Guimaraes was admired by Arteta, who had made it clear he wanted proven talent to take his starting XI - rather than the wider squad - to greater heights.

Berta used his strong relationship with Guimaraes' representatives to facilitate Arsenal's move, hence why Newcastle maintained they had had no direct contact from the London club until days before his move was completed.

It is not uncommon for Berta to lean on intermediaries to conduct negotiations, although the approach has had varying degrees of success.

For instance, Arsenal actively sought moves for Leicester City teenagers Jeremy Monga and Louis Page over the summer.

But sources insist that the lack of club-to-club discussions meant both players ultimately did not join Arsenal, with Monga eventually signing for Manchester City when he appeared to be on the verge of moving to the Emirates.

That said, Berta's success in pivoting the club towards a deal for Guimaraes when it became clear other targets were not viable was well received behind the scenes at Arsenal.

The signing of Ezri Konsa was equally complex. Konsa was viewed internally as Arteta's first-choice defensive option.

Arteta wanted players used to the rigours of Premier League football - hence the moves for Guimaraes, Konsa and the failed efforts to land Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.

Konsa's ability to play at right-back was also viewed as a major benefit. Arsenal considered signing an orthodox right-back, with Ivan Fresneda among the options, but Konsa's versatility was a key factor.

But Berta appeared reluctant to meet Villa's valuation. A week before the Konsa deal was confirmed, Arsenal made a Â£40m offer, which was duly rejected.

Sources claim the deal was eventually sealed by the ownership at both clubs, and the transfer was agreed at Â£51m, with Â£4m in add-ons.

In the event of not reaching an agreement for Konsa, it is understood Tottenham duo Cristian Romero and Micky van der Ven were identified as targets â but Arsenal's north London rivals would not consider selling to them.

Como centre-back Jacobo Ramon is a player the club will continue to monitor, but clauses attached to his current contract make the deal difficult.

Tarik Muharemovic, who joined Leeds United, was another considered.

In attack, Christos Tzolis' impact since arriving from Club Brugge in a deal worth about Â£35m means the Greece international has been heralded as one of the discoveries of the summer.

It is understood the potential deal for the former Norwich winger was initially raised by an intermediary close to a senior member of the coaching staff during the close season.

Berta's number two, Maurizio Micheli, watched Tzolis play for his country against Sweden in June and was suitably impressed.

So far, the 24-year-old looks a positive addition to Arteta's squad.

Arsenal, who also made Piero Hincapie's loan deal permanent and signed Illan Meslier on a free transfer, are happy with the signings they have made.

The captures of Guimaraes and Konsa, who will both be 30 by the end of next season, have raised eyebrows given the combined Â£126m fee, amid concerns over how the pair's longevity may impact the natural evolution of the squad.

Yet it is undeniable that Guimares and Konsa add elite quality and experience to Arsenal ranks, and ultimately the club feel they paid the going rate to get those deals over the line.

Vinicius Jr signed a new six-year deal at Real Madrid in August

While the club delivered proven talent for Arteta in defence and midfield, Berta's remit of adding an elite attacker ended in disappointment.

Rogers was the club's primary target heading into the window, and the early indications were positive amid a strongly held view internally that the forward wanted to join.

At the start of the summer, it was Arsenal's understanding that Villa valued Rogers at Â£100m. Arsenal valued Rogers at Â£80m.

Berta, however, was confident of negotiating the price down to a level he and the club believed could get the deal done.

In the meantime, however, Berta explored alternatives - Bradley Barcola, Kenan Yildiz, Yan Diomande and Nico Paz were admired.

Anthony Gordon was a long-term target, but he had agreed before the World Cup to join Barcelona.

Yildiz and Paz will continue to be realistic targets moving forward. Eli Junior Kroupi is another the club will watch once he returns from injury for Bournemouth.

Anderson's move from Forest to City for Â£116m, however, altered the complexion of Villa's outlook on Rogers' future.

Villa increased their valuation to Â£120m and ultimately Chelsea ended up signing the attacker for Â£117m.

Arsenal, it is understood, were given the opportunity to match Chelsea's offer but refused, believing their Â£80m valuation was fair - but it does beg the question of whether Rogers would be a Gunners player now if Berta had acted sooner.

Ultimately, the failure to land Rogers arrived as the first of a series of blows to Berta in his efforts to deliver a top-class left-sided attacker for the team.

Arsenal genuinely believed they had a realistic chance of signing Vinicius Jr before he decided to sign a new contract at Real Madrid.

Berta and Arteta were all in on the Brazil icon. The club were prepared finance the deal too.

While the transfer would likely have cost a British record fee and been one of the most lucrative remuneration packages in Premier League history, the benefit to Arteta's team and the Brazil superstar's commercial value meant Arsenal were absolutely prepared to complete the deal.

Yet well-placed sources expressed to BBC Sport over the summer that Vinicius did not want to leave Real, while others feared Arsenal were being used to strengthen the attacker's efforts to secure a more lucrative contract at the Bernabeu.

Those concerns came to fruition as Vinicius signed a new long-term contract in Spain in another Arsenal disappointment.

There were similar reservations about Arsenal's well-documented pursuit of Julian Alvarez.

The Atletico Madrid forward showed very little indication that he was willing to join Arsenal; his preference to join Barcelona was one of the worst-kept secrets of the window.

But Atletico's point-blank refusal to sell to Barcelona was deemed reason enough by Berta and Arteta to persist with their interest in the hope of Alvarez changing his mind until the closing days of the window.

Alvarez, however, preferred to stay at Atletico, even though his relationship with the club is at an all-time low.

Did Arsenal waste their time with Vinicius and Alvarez? The answer varies depending on who you speak to.

When it became clear Alvarez was unlikely, Berta explored his options.

Intriguingly, Arsenal have admired Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who was deemed not for sale over the summer, although there were concerns over how he would fit into Arteta's system.

It is claimed Berta relies significantly on his vast network of agent connections rather than acting on the club's existing scouting information when analysing the market.

For example, last summer, when all the scouting information pointed towards a move for Benjamin Sesko, Berta's arrival meant the club pivoted to Viktor Gyokeres, who is currently second-choice striker.

This summer the club's late dalliance with Lyon winger Malick Fofana provided a further example of Berta leaning on his agency connections after management agency Roc Nation offered Arsenal an opportunity to sign the Belgium international.

Berta's relationship with Roc Nation was particularly prevalent this summer given Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius and the sale of Gabriel Martinelli, who are both clients of the agency.

It remains to be seen how much of an impact Arsenal's failure to sign a recognised top-level attacker impacts their season, particularly in light of Martinelli and Leandro Trossard's departures.

Arsenal headed into the window with a clear remit of ensuring the club become more sustainable and adept at trading.

Part of that directive is to ensure the club remain compliant with domestic and European financial regulations.

Depending on who you talk to, the size of the potential deals for Vinicius or Alvarez would have raised doubts over Arsenal's ability to stay within the regulations.

Nevertheless, ensuring they maximised the benefits of player trading will become an increasing part of Arsenal's financial operation in the future.

There was already evidence of that through the sale of Martinelli, whose Â£60m exit to Al-Hilal was the club's record departure. Arsenal have also secured a sell-on clause in the deal.

The exits of Martinelli, Trossard, Gabriel Jesus, Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Fabio Vieira and Karl Hein secured the club in the region of Â£114m.

Through intermediaries, a possible exit for Myles Lewis-Skelly was explored, with a fee of about Â£80m believed to have been mooted for the midfielder.

Manchester United, who were attracted to Lewis-Skelly's ability to play at left-back, were interested but ultimately deemed his valuation too high.

Of course, it is Berta's job to have a firm grasp on the level of interest in the club's players and their market value but, nevertheless, the thought of Lewis-Skelly's departure resulted in huge uproar from supporters.

As BBC Sport revealed last month, the Gunners resisted any temptation to sell Ethan Nwaneri on a permanent deal, the academy graduate landing a season-long loan deal to Borussia Dortmund that includes a January recall option if required.

The minimum Â£15m fee secured in Trossard's deal to Besiktas is also viewed as a good deal inside the Emirates given the Belgian turns 32 in December.

Having spent nearly Â£450m in 12 months, Berta's work in the market has helped the club deliver their first league title in 22 years.

Yet, despite the money splashed, there remain clear issues in the squad - certainly in attack.

The summer window has left many supporters questioning Berta's body of work at Arsenal.

And with the average age of the squad increasing following the captures of Konsa and Guimaraes, can the current options build a dynasty of success before the club need to spend heavily again on regenerating the team?

Are Arsenal taking a risk in not signing a world-class forward?

#1100. Exiled Jack Grealish RETURNS to Everton training after being dropped following boozy nights at pubs and karaoke: Ex-England star could be back in team after international break

Published: 12:34 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 14:16 EDT, 6 November 2026

Jack Grealish will return to Everton training after being dropped and exiled by David Moyes.

The 31-year-old was axed for back-to-back matches against Newcastle following a 'breach of club discipline' and is not part of the Toffees' matchday squad for the third game on the spin when they host Coventry tonight.

Grealish, who has made seven appearances since re-joining Everton for a second season-long loan spell from Man City in the summer, had been banished since failing to show up for a training session on Monday last week. It is understood staff struggled to make contact with the winger.

Grealish will now be reintegrated on a tailored training programme to regain match fitness and could be included in first-team sessions during the international break from next week.

Grealish had made four successive starts before he missed Everton's 2-0 defeat by Arsenal on October 24 due to illness.

Grealish was reported to have had back-to-back nights out prior to the Toffees' defeat in north London.

Jack Grealish, previously pictured out with a friend, was exiled by Everton but is now set to return to training with the team

David Moyes could start Grealish against Brentford after the international break

The three-time Premier League winner attended the Pride of Britain awards at the Grosvenor House hotel in London on October 19 where he presented the Child of Courage award to 12-year-old Zac Howells.

He is then reported to have finished the night of celebration off at Bam Karaoke Box, a karaoke hotspot in Victoria, central London.

According to the Sun, he stayed up until the early hours of the morning singing with his friends and enjoying the drinks on offer.

The next day, Grealish is believed to have returned to Cheshire, where he and many of his footballer friends live, to meet team-mates Jordan Pickford and Tyler Dibling at The Mauldeth pub in Wilmslow.

The trio, joined by Grealish's former City team-mate and captain Kyle Walker, where they watched Paris Saint-Germain's thrilling Champions League victory over Barcelona. A witness claimed to the Sun that they enjoyed a few drinks.

Moyes had been coy on the situation when asked about it on Thursday. He said: 'You probably know I'm not going to give any details, it is a club decision and I support that decision (for him to be punished). It is something I don't want to speak too much about.

'The one thing about Everton is that we have got really good values behind it. All the players stand up to the values and accept the values, on the pitch and off the pitch. From that point of view, I think the players did a brilliant job.'

Without Grealish once again, Everton are seeking to secure a third win in a row when they come up against former Toffees boss Frank Lampard and his Coventry team.

Grealish is reported to have gone on consecutive nights out after attending the Pride of Britain Awards on October 19

After the Coventry clash, Everton are next in Premier League action at Gtech Community Stadium against Brentford on November 23.

Grealish will be targeting a return in that fixture and hope he can begin to rebuild his relationship with Moyes over the next three weeks.

He has played for England 39 times and turned out for Everton on 22 occasions, scoring twice and providing six assists, with a nasty foot injury cut short his campaign last term.

#1099. Author or artificial intelligence? Literature in crisis

AI is a hot topic at this year's Frankfurt Book Fair. An international literary scandal has raised questions about machine-generated texts.

It's the hot-button topic at the Frankfurt Book Fair: How profoundly will artificial intelligence (AI) transform the book industry, and how can this transformation be regulated?

Given the warnings about the technology's long-term risks to humanity as a whole, such debates might appear rather narrow in scope. In reality, however, they concern very concrete issues — copyright protection, the power of tech giants and the future of creativity. Many agree that the political measures taken don't go far enough.

This year, however, another aspect has entered the debate: Can we actually recognize when a text has been written with the help of artificial intelligence, and if so, can this be proven?

These are some of the questions raised by the current scandal surrounding Haitian-Canadian author Thelyson Orelien and his debut novel, "C'etait ca ou mourir," (This title means "It Was Either That or Die" in English but an English translation has not yet been published), which was published in Canada in the spring.

The book about global migration was universally acclaimed, with translation rights sold in more than 20 languages. Soon after the book was published in France, it was long-listed for the prestigious Prix Goncourt.

But then, all of a sudden, allegations emerged that the book had been written almost entirely using AI. Orelien, a rising literary star, found himself branded a fraud despite denying all the allegations. His nomination for the Goncourt was withdrawn.

So, who should we believe? An author or an AI that claims to have identified AI-generated writing?

"We will have to learn to live with doubt," said Hannes Bajohr, a professor of German literature at the University of California, Berkeley.

Bajohr has spent years examining how AI is changing both writing and reading. His prediction: If the origins of texts can no longer be reliably established, we will have to evaluate them differently. What matters will be their quality alone, rather than whether AI was used in the writing process.

Nina George, a bestselling author and the honorary president of the European Writers' Council, is unwilling to accept this.

At the Frankfurt Book Fair, she was awarded the Friedrich Perthes Prize in recognition of her commitment to issues such as AI and copyright reform.

George has addressed the European Parliament and the lower house of the German parliament, speaking and writing tirelessly about the dangers of AI models. It is perverse, she said, that an author should suddenly have to prove that their writing is the creation of a human. The focus of her campaigns are the tech corporations' self-serving mentality and copyright protection.

But what if an author sees AI not as an enemy but as a tool that makes writing easier?

US author and artist Luke Stoffel deliberately used AI in his memoir, "How To Win One Million Dollars and Shit Glitter," and was open about doing so.

"I'm dyslexic," he said in a video interview. "I've always written and made up stories, but I never dared to take them any further."

It was only with the help of AI, he said, that he was able to fulfill his dream. The technology drew his attention to weaknesses in his writing and suggested a marketing strategy that actually worked.

In May 2026, he received an award from the Independent Book Publishers Association for the book.

For South African author Coral Hart, AI is actually the foundation of her business model. Publishing under various pseudonyms, each year she releases more than 200 different novels, spanning the genres of romance, thriller and mystery.

Hart sees herself as an ideas person, as well as an editor and publisher. Although none of her books has yet become a bestseller, the business is profitable, she said, adding that each book reaches more than 5,000 people.

Stoffel considers the entire debate hypocritical and points out that many publishers have been working with AI tools for some time. He's certain that "right now, a million-copy bestseller is being printed that was created with the help of AI. The author won't admit it, and then there'll be a scandal."

It is entirely possible that the scandal surrounding Thelyson Orelien is precisely that story. But we may never know for sure.

For now, the battle against the tech giants continues, some of which are themselves increasingly concerned about losing control.

At the very start of the Frankfurt fair, the German Publishers and Booksellers Association issued an appeal to policymakers in Berlin and Brussels, calling for stricter regulation of artificial intelligence, which they said is more urgent than ever. More than 140 publishers have signed it.

But for now, it remains just an appeal. And the question of what authors themselves should be permitted to do with AI will undoubtedly continue to fuel debates in the future.

#1098. A team that offered hope... then, four months later, Hamas attacked Israel

A team that offered hope... then, four months later, Hamas attacked Israel

It was, says Ido Rakovsky, like reporting on "science fiction", rather than sport.

Israel, whose senior team have qualified for the World Cup just once, had beaten global powerhouses Brazil in the quarter-finals of the under-20 version of the tournament.

At the final whistle, the commentator covering the match for Israeli television vowed "you will tell of this night to your children, and they will tell it to your grandchildren".

Five days later, the team's semi-final against Uruguay was the most-watched thing of the evening on Israeli television, drawing a 23% viewing share.

Politicians clamoured to congratulate the team.

"That summer, everybody was watching under-20 football, everybody knew the players," says Rakovsky, who was covering the team for Israeli media outlet Haaretz.

"Everybody in Israel fell in love with these kids."

It wasn't just their deeds on the pitch that felt otherworldly, though.

After scoring a stoppage-time winner against Uzbekistan in the last 16, Anan Khalaili had given an interview to Israeli television.

In it Khalaili, an Israeli Arab, thanked the viewers back home for staying up late to watch his team win in Argentina.

To do so, he used the words 'Am Yisrael' - a Hebrew phrase that means 'People of Israel' and is bound up in Jewish religion, community, culture and history.

"That an Arab player used that figure of speech said something about the identity of that team," says Rakovsky.

"That team made real the claim that football can really bring people together - that Muslim players are part of the national team of the Jewish state, representing Israel and creating something better, both for the present and future."

But a little over four months after Khalaili's interview and the win over Brazil, Hamas attacked Israel.

The armed Palestinian group killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza. The United Nations believes the retaliation has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians., external

As the war goes on, can the potential of a golden generation of Israel's footballers, in sport and society, be realised?

Israel beat Brazil 3-2 in the quarter-finals of the U20 World Cup in 2023

Beaten 1-0 by eventual champions Uruguay, Israel finished third at that Under-20 World Cup in 2023.

The same set of players, with a few additions and omissions, had already impressed at continental level.

They were runners-up at 2022's Under-19 Euros, beaten by England in extra-time in the final, and would go on to make the semi-finals of 2023's Under-20 Euros.

Israel has produced outstanding players in the past. Eyal Berkovic and Yossi Benayoun were technical, gifted attackers with long Premier League careers.

But a depth of talent, emerging together, sets the current cohort apart.

Khalaili has been one of the most sought-after young prospects in Europe this summer.

After his Â£21.5m move to Inter Milan fell through, Crystal Palace saw off competition from Nottingham Forest to pick him up for a similar fee from Belgian side Union Saint-Gilloise.

Playmaker Oscar Gloukh, 22, wears Ajax's number 10 shirt after his form earned a move from Red Bull Salzburg.

Left-back Roy Revivo signed for Spanish club Elche on transfer deadline day this month from Maccabi Tel Aviv, while Twente defender Stav Lemkin, also 23, is also highly rated.

Dor Turgeman, Ilay Feingold and Idan Toklomati are impressing in Major League Soccer in the United States.

All have now won full caps, but were moulded into a collective, cohesive unit - something that has often been beyond the senior side - by Israel's age-grade coach Ofir Haim.

"It isn't an issue at all here," Haim said, external of the different backgrounds in his squad during the 2023 Under-20 World Cup.

"We don't have any problem with religion. Not at all. We have players here who put on tefillin [Jewish ceremonial wear, containing verses from the Torah] - and Anan [Khalaili], Hamza [Shibli] and Ahmed [Salman] perform the Muslim prayers.

"We don't even talk about this. We unite everybody, and I wish the country were as united as this team."

Ofir Haim managed various domestic teams in Israel before becoming head coach of the U19s and U20s

Football has long been the part of Israeli society where communities mix together who may not otherwise meet.

"The majority of the Jewish people who arrived in the mandate period [a spell between 1923 and 1948 where the region was run by Britain] emigrated from Europe," says Dr Omer Einav, a historian and author of Defending the Goal, a book on Israel's football history.

"They were Europeans and when you think about cinema, music, theatre, dance, they had nothing in common with Middle Eastern culture. Nothing, except football. That was the only common language, the only thing they both love in the same way."

Encouraged by the British administrators who ran the region, teams from different communities, and some made up of elements of each, would play against each other.

When the modern state of Israel was formed in 1948, much of the Arab population that remained inside its borders continued to identify as or with Palestinians. Most still do.

They are also an intrinsic part of Israeli football.

While they make up 20% of Israel's population, they represent about 35% of those involved in the sport at elite level nationally.

The first Arab player to represent Israel's national team was Rifaat Turk in 1976. In 2018, Bibars Natcho became the first Muslim to captain the team.

Turk was roundly abused. Natcho's decision not to sing Israel's national anthem, the lyrics of which relate to the Jewish search for a homeland, was condemned by some., external

For a short time in the summer of 2023, it seemed as if Haim's under-20 side might offer a watershed moment of unity and co-existence.

But football, like everything in Israel, changed on 7 October.

Israel came second in their group at the U20 World Cup and went on to finish third in the tournament

Matan Segal directed Kick It Out Israel, an anti-discrimination initiative with similar aims but no link to the English organisation of the same name, for almost four years before stepping down a few months ago.

Racism has long been present in Israeli club football. Beitar Jerusalem's fans are among the most notorious.

In 2013, ultras burned down their own club's offices in protest at the signing of two Chechen Muslims.

The most extreme Beitar fans have long taunted Israeli Arabs with chants of "may your village burn", while declaring themselves "forever pure".

However during his time at Kick It Out Israel, Segal saw racism against Arab players become more virulent and widespread.

Covid, during which fans radicalised online during lockdown, was one cause.

The election of Israel's far-right government at the end of 2022, legitimising views towards Palestinians that were previously seen as extreme, was a second.

"Before 7 October, people generally respected the Arab players," Segal said.

"Even though they had difficulties with them not singing the Israeli anthem, they respected them and they could talk about it.

"After 7 October though, we saw an increase in racist remarks.

"It was happening at small clubs where we hadn't seen it before. There were terrible songs - 'Let's kill all Arabs', 'There are no schools in Gaza because there are no children left'."

Football, inevitably, has become a focal point for emotion generated by the conflict.

Clubs which are usually bitter rivals came together to remember those killed by Hamas. Scarves were part of the commemoration at the site of the Nova music festival, where hundreds were killed.

Hapoel Jerusalem's club badge now features a silhouette of Hersh Goldberg-Polin, who was abducted and killed in captivity and whose parents have campaigned for peace through their grief.

Meanwhile, Israeli Defence Force (IDF) soldiers have posed with club flags and banners while on operation in Gaza, dedicating their actions to the clubs and ultras back home., external

In such a heightened atmosphere, young footballers â closely connected to the conflict through Israel's programme of national service and a barrage of online commentary and images â are under constant scrutiny and pressure.

Gloukh's lifelong friend Afik Tery was killed by a Hamas explosive while serving in the IDF.

After his death, Gloukh posted a poignant set of pictures, external of the pair arm-in-arm over time - as young boys at birthday parties, as young men at a wedding - with the final slide showing Tery's funeral.

Among the online replies were the taunts of pro-Palestinians.

For Israel players with Palestinian heritage, the stakes are especially and dangerously high.

Dia Saba plays in a similar playmaking role to Gloukh. The 33-year-old has scored three goals in 13 appearances for Israel.

He is unlikely ever to add to that tally.

Saba was one of Maccabi Haifa's most high-profile stars when, at the start of the conflict, his wife Narmin posted a message to Instagram.

"There are children in Gaza, too," she wrote.

Saba apologised for the outrage caused, but could not save his career in Israel. He left Maccabi Haifa in 2025 and now plays for Turkish side Amedspor.

"My dream was to play for Maccabi Haifa, the club that I support, the team that I grew up with," Saba said at the time.

"I wanted to continue. But sometimes there are reasons that are stronger than us that don't allow it."

Former Israel Under-21 player Ataa Jaber (right) switched nationalities to represent Palestine in June 2023

Saba and others are used to having their loyalty questioned. From all sides.

Many in the Arab world would like more Palestinian prospects within Israel to follow the example of Ataa Jaber.

Jaber captained Israel's Under-21 side but switched nationalities, external to represent Palestine in June 2023, saying he could no longer separate sport and politics after seeing police evict Palestinian families from their homes in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem.

Switching away from a high level of international football damaged his prospects of a move to Europe. At home, there were calls for his Israeli citizenship to be revoked. But, for Jaber, it was preferable to representing a country whose actions he deplored.

Those footballers who voice an opinion on the conflict choose their words carefully.

Beram Kayal, the former Brighton, Celtic and Israel player, knows the dilemmas and reality well.

"To be Arabic in Israel, it's sometimes hard," he says. "Sometimes it is tough.

"Opportunities-wise, sometimes we are not on the same level."

However, he believes in a pluralistic future for Israel and football as a tool to achieve it.

His friendship with Tomer Hemed - whom he first met as a young teenager at Maccabi Haifa's academy and later played alongside at Brighton and Charlton, as well as international level - sums up his approach.

"When I played with Tomer, he prayed like this," he says, touching his hand to his back of his head to indicate a kippah, the small skullcap worn as a sign of Jewish faith.

"And I was praying for Allah," he adds, raising his arms above his shoulders in worship.

"He was my team-mate and he is my brother.

"In football, on the pitch, you never look at colour, culture or religion. You just want the best people around you to win the game."

The 38-year-old is now employed by Israel's Football Association to work with young talents from Palestinian areas.

In doing so he works alongside former Israel goalkeeper Boni Ginzburg, who played across Glasgow at Rangers and is now the IFA's technical director.

After Arabic was relegated behind Hebrew as Israel's official language by a controversial 2018 law promoted by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the IFA put on Hebrew language lessons for Arabic-speaking coaches to ensure they could still obtain their qualifications.

"Not in our building," says Kayal when asked about the precedence given to Hebrew.

"I'm in this place [the IFA] to bring the culture of the Arabic people to the table.

"I say to the Arabic players when they come into the national team: Speak in your language, don't be afraid, don't be shy to speak, don't just afraid to show yourself.

"Israel is a young country. We need to learn from our DNA, to see the different between the Jewish, the Circassians, the Arabic, the Muslim, the Christian, the Druze â all the colours â put that together and learn what we could do better."

Israel are aiming to qualify for Euro 2028

Israel's aim is to go better than their national team has managed in more than 50 years.

Ran Ben-Shimon was appointed as the senior side's head coach in 2024. He was given the goal of converting youthful promise into qualification for Euro 2028, which will be staged in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

Success would place more stress on Israel's players and, potentially, squad unity.

Large-scale protests are planned for Republic of Ireland's forthcoming Nations League matches with Israel. Dublin will host seven games at the tournament.

Villa Park in Birmingham, from which Maccabi Tel Aviv fans were banned from attending a Europa League match in November, will stage four matches.

Hampden Park, two miles across Glasgow from where Celtic fans have held vociferous pro-Palestine protests, has six.

Wherever Israel play, players will be confronted with criticism of their country's treatment of Palestinians, both at home and in Gaza, that is rarely voiced at home.

"Israelis are very sensitive to anyone showing any kind of sympathy for what happened on 7 October," says Dr Sophia Solomon, part of Ben-Gurion University's Center for Sports Diplomacy.

"It is like denying the Holocaust, that is the proportion of it. A war is a special situation, it wasn't like this before, but to express your agony became more encouraged as we saw the European arena become more anti-Israeli.

"One reaction ignited another and there is more obligation to identify yourself with the victims of 7 October."

She believes that it will take time for Israeli society, footballers included, to understand the past three years and speak openly about the conflict.

"Until the ongoing war ends, no-one can say what he thinks," she said. "Even after the Middle East returns to its 'normal' craziness, maybe it will take a decade to pass before people can start talking about their experiences and expectations.

"Time has to pass until you can touch certain areas, and at the moment you can see a lot of avoidance about talking about it, even mentioning it."

Anan Khalaili, who scored in Israel's Under-20 World Cup victory over Brazil in 2023, joined Crystal Palace this summer

The time for this stellar generation to fulfil their potential may come before that.

It may not. Translating youth-level promise to senior-level product is never simple.

But, whatever the future holds, for a few months, in the summer of 2023, Haim and his team gave Israel something special.

"We saw Anan Khalaili and Hamza Shibli scoring against Brazil and that was our hope, that was the future. That was our future," says Einav.

"I'm not so optimistic, but people thought maybe it's really a magical thing that can help Israeli society in general.

"There was something there, something new, something where people said 'OK, if we co-operate, if we work together, we can also succeed in sport.'

"That's what we all care about, right? We want to be good at sports. We are sick of watching the World Cup from our living room.

"I think football is in some isolated, sterilised dimension - some kind of bubble - inside Israeli society. It is not hermetic. A lot of dirt comes in - racism, violence - but I do believe that football can reflect good things that can happen. The equality of chances, the tolerance and solidarity of all people living here.

"It can't heal anything but it can help us see one another in a more human way.

"So, yeah there was definitely a moment, but it was before our world changed and collapsed."

Only time will tell what remains of that moment and whether it can be revived.

#1097. Hapless and hopeless Man Utd bring curtain down on out-of-depth Carrick

Hapless, hopeless and utterly humiliated. And that has to be that for Michael Carrick. It is surely inconceivable that he will continue any longer as Manchester United’s head coach. A proud club on its knees and a favoured son on his way out.

The former midfielder will carry the can. As managers always do. Even if the fault lines run so deep at United that it feels like they are almost irreparable. Owners – the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe – executives, players. A collective failing of monumental proportions. Although, again, it will be the manager who goes. Carrick knows it and it looked like it at the end. He knows the score, especially after this score.

More than four years ago Ralf Rangnick, the then interim manager, declared that United needed “open heart surgery”. Now there is barely a pulse.

An announcement must be imminent, with United turning to someone else in the fight against Premier League relegation. A joke? No, this abject performance against Bournemouth leaves United in 16th place, just a point above the bottom three, so the priority for the new man will be clear. Save them from the drop. They are 14 points off the top already, but forget that. It is irrelevant given their plight.

That is how far United have, once again, fallen. Fans in the Stretford End unfurled their “Standards” banner, bearing the faces of Eric Cantona, Roy Keane and Bryan Robson.

It was first revealed in December 2021 in Carrick’s final match as interim following Ole Gunnar Solskjaer’s sacking. This should be his final game again, under different, more traumatic, circumstances.

If it is, he is going out having made a stand. He dropped Bruno Fernandes for his outspoken comments, aimed directly at Carrick and his tactics, following the dismal 4-1 Champions League defeat away to Como on Wednesday.

At 2-0 down here it was telling that Carrick turned to Matheus Cunha when he substituted Youri Tielemans, who had been so terribly slow and ineffective, at half-time. Carrick did not bring on Fernandes. And he did not turn to the captain after, as he made four substitutions, including bringing on 19-year-old Shea Lacey. That said it all.

The television cameras catching Omar Berrada, the United chief executive, shaking his head in the stands as Carrick’s team gave away goals also told its own story. They have two wins from 12 in all competitions and none in eight. They have only beaten newly promoted Ipswich Town, in August, and Azerbaijan minnows Sabah this season. United were so careless it looked like they could not care less.

There was no guarantee, after Como, that Carrick would remain in charge after this game. So, losing and losing so embarrassingly – it was three, it should have been five – has to have obvious consequences. However cherished Carrick is. However much the fans excuse him. Yes, he has not been helped enough, but he has also not been good enough.

Finishing third and qualifying for the Champions League last season has proved to be the kind of bounce a new manager can achieve, after the pressure was relieved by the sacking of Ruben Amorim, rather than something more sustainable. There was always the fear that Carrick, despite his playing pedigree, might be out of his depth in this job. And so it is proving to be. Especially as he has been hung out to dry. Carrick certainly appeared resigned to his fate.

But what is he coaching? What is he trying to do with United? How does he want his team to play? Yes, there are limitations, but they are badly set up, tactically poor, and struggle to build attacks. The players are not responding, but it does not mean Carrick is blameless.

Bournemouth were not just collectively and individually better – and despite how good they are, that is some indictment of United – but better organised. They knew what they were doing, believed in it and relished it as they collected a fourth victory, and a fourth clean sheet in a row, after a slow start under Marco Rose, the new head coach. It was no shock.

The nature of the goals spoke volumes. For the first, a free-kick was needlessly conceded by Ayden Heaven, who endured a particularly difficult game, as he lunged in recklessly, forcing Evanilson to jump out of the way or risk injury.

Justin Kluivert whipped the ball in beyond the far post and it was met by Rayan, who volleyed in low and precise. The Brazilian was unmarked. Carrick protested – at what? – and the Bournemouth supporters sang “you’re getting sacked in the morning”.

What a finish from Rayan to give Bournemouth the lead! 🔥 https://t.co/9BV0G5Tqgi

The outstanding Rayan should have had a hat-trick but failed to take two chances in the second half, when he only had goalkeeper Senne Lammens to beat, after Bournemouth had already doubled their lead. It came as Leny Yoro slipped over and presented the ball straight to Adrien Truffert, who squared it for Marcus Tavernier to side-foot home. It was that ridiculously easy.

The third was the same, with Evanilson chasing down a ball forward by Tyler Adams. The striker should not have got there. But Harry Maguire, captain in Fernandes’s absence, gave up, pointing at Lammens to win it. Instead, the goalkeeper was beaten to the ball and Evanilson’s finish from an angle, arcing high into the net, was superb.

"What a finish!" 😮‍💨 Evanilson makes it 3-0 to Bournemouth with a stunning goal https://t.co/hPMR78Z3cX

“You’re going down with the City,” goaded the Bournemouth fans and it is that end of the table United need to fret about. Which means, for Carrick, it has to be over. The Stretford End sang his name. But it was out of support for him as a player, his reputation, what he represented, not what is happening now as they once again vented their anger at the owners, director of football, Jason Wilcox, and even the plans for a new stadium.

It was the same as Carrick walked down the tunnel, thumping his chest as his name was sung. Then it turned. The vitriol, frustration and anger dripped down on the players, washing them away.

This felt like a new nadir. And the need for yet another new start away to Chelsea on Saturday.

Former Tottenham defender speaking to the BBC:

Manchester United’s players were just standing there today. I did not see in their body language that they are prepared to do everything for the manager, the club or the fans to change their situation.

It’s an easy thing to say they are lacking leaders but it’s true. They just don’t have big characters. It is not something technical but if you are in a tunnel and you saw the likes of [former Man Utd defenders] Nemanja Vidic or Rio Ferdinand their body language told the opposition that they were going to have a tough afternoon.

Carrick admits he does not know if he will remain in place.

The club have a week off now, with the next match a trip to Stamford Bridge against a tasty Chelsea side, albeit one who lost to Spurs last night.

He says: “It’s a tough situation. What is next? I don’t know. I’ll always do what’s best for this football club. I don’t change that now. I love what I do. I love the responsibility. But we’ll have to wait and see.”

Carrick gives a non-answer over his choice to leave Fernandes on the bench.

He says: “There’s always times when you’re trying to make decisions that are to change the course of play and made a difference but those are the decisions we made today.”

Carrick then denies that his acknowledgement of the crowd was to say goodbye, adding: “It wasn’t a farewell from me. I’m mixed emotions, I’m feeling it for my players, they’re going through a tough spell.

“Some of it we can help, some of it the situation unravels and the boys are feeling it at the moment. Mixed emotions for the supporters to respond in that way.”

Carrick also tells Sky: “It’s really difficult to have a day like this at this football club and feel the emotion and dynamics of what it was like today.

“Not for me personally but for Manchester United. It was really mixed. I feel responsibility with the position I’m in. I’ve been at the club a long time. It hurts a lot going through this.”

Carrick potentially acknowledges that his time is up, telling Sky: “It was a strange, mixed of emotions at the end of the game. It wasn’t a nice way to end the game.

“It was a tough day for the players. We went into the game having been rocked. You can feel that. They’re really hurting and disappointed in there. It’s not a nice feeling. You have to accept it, we’re in that situation.”

Today’s United captain Harry Maguire tells Sky Sports: “It wasn’t good enough. Disappointed to give a goal away so early - another set play - and conceding first in the Premier League it makes it difficult.

“A mistake for the second makes it hard for ourselves. We didn’t perform well enough as individuals or as a team and we didn’t deserve anything from the game.

“It’s not clicking at the moment. Results are not good enough and performances in the last week not good enough. Still early in the season.

“Got to find something, question yourself, look in the mirror - that’s the most important thing - think what you can do more and what more you can contribute to the team and if we do that we’ll get somewhere.”

United players have said this for some time now. Each season they look in the mirror, and each season the supporters get the same.

Telegraph columnist Jamie Carragher thinks Carrick has had enough after that.

His emotional exit after the match suggested as much, with the former Liverpool player telling Sky: “He wants to be put out of his misery tonight.”

The fact that a mid-table team can come to Old Trafford and leave with three points is no longer a surprise.

If anything, it’s unusual when competent teams struggle against United these days.

Quite how replacing a manager changes a decade of falling short solves things, who knows?

At least the scoreline is not a surprise. Bournemouth always tend to win 3-0 at Old Trafford these days

Arne Slot underwhelmed last season, and Liverpool moved swiftly to appoint Andoni Iraola from Bournemouth.

They have defeated an impressive Brighton side 2-0 today, and you can read our report here.

Former Manchester United winger Ashley Young is scathing about the players who have succeeded him.

He told Sky Sports: “Unfortunately for Michael Carrick, it’s so disappointing. The fans are behind him and backing him and of course they are, because he’s a legend of the football club.

“But the players on the pitch showed nothing. They didn’t run, they didn’t look like a team together.

“If you looked at the difference to the Bournemouth team, you’d swap every single player for that Manchester United team. It was a poor showing.”

Extraordinary scenes at the end here. Carrick walks around the pitch waving at the fans and being applauded back. It felt very much like a manager saying goodbye. As he reached the Stretford End they start singing his song and Carrick responds by banging his chest in front of them. But as soon as the manager disappeared down the tunnel the fans instantly turned on the players trailing behind. A crescendo of sustained boos reverberate around as they target the players and make their feelings quite clear.

Picking Fernandes on the bench meant that Carrick got to snub him, but it also means that Sky get to make a point of his efforts to express himself, which does not really help the situation.

The away side now match Manchester City and Liverpool.

3 - This is the third time that Bournemouth gone 3-0 up in a Premier League game at Old Trafford (also in December 2023 and December 2024). Only Liverpool and Man City have done so as many times in the competition (3). Dreamers. https://t.co/6EO4byrwCw

United started poorly, got worse, and the less said about the rest, the better.

Two wins, the last against Sabah in the Champions League, and the other against Ipswich Town.

It’s damning. As Fernandes goes down the tunnel, there are hints of jeers for him from the crowd, too.

The camera cuts to Jason Wilcox in the stands, and Neville observes the decision to sack Carrick, which is likely in the post, will “disgust” fans.

After that win, United are in the bottom six.

Manchester United are soundly beaten for the second time in a week.

Como were hugely impressive in the Champions League. Bournemouth were effective but not special. United managed to regress in short order.

Boos ring out, but the crowd then go back to chanting Carrick’s name. They blame someone else for the troubles.

Neville ponders why United did not buy a left-back, with Dalot playing there once again. He has actually been fairly competent today. The midfielders - who were bought this summer - were probably the least impressive. Andrey Santos and Tielemans have been poor.

Carrick will probably get a decent reception, because most of the venom has been aimed at the owners rather than the head coach.

Jason Wilcox is getting some charming chants about him too, now, and he has shaped a poor squad, going by results.

Five minutes are indicated for the rest of the match. Bournemouth look likelier to get a fourth than United are for a first.

Diakite comes on for the last 30 seconds of normal time, after Smith had dawdled. The United fans are starting to leave in greater numbers now, into the rain.

Kroupi comes on, Smith, Tavernier and Evanilson off. Adli is on, but Diakite is yet to replace Smith, who took too long to come off.

Santos strains to reach a Lacey cross, stood up well to the back post, and wins a corner.

Bournemouth struggle to clear it quickly, but United can’t force a chance.

Bournemouth are sitting back, confident of the three points. United have shown so little today they can hardly be worried.

Lacey is coming on now. Still no Fernandes. Carrick clearly prepared to go down sending a message.

Gary Neville says the situation has turned, “sour,” decrying the summer failure not to buy better midfielders.

Lacey comes on for Amad, who has been very quiet. So no Fernandes.

United are reduced to shooting from distance against the legs of Bournemouth defenders.

Carrick was waiting to bring on Zirkzee has Bournemouth scored their third. Even as United sink to a new low, the United manager seems to be making a point by not bringing on Fernandes. Ratcliffe and the Glazers both being targeted.

Christie on for Cook, and Zirkzee for Baleba.

A long ball holds the ball up as the keeper rushes to intercept. He’s stuck, and Evanilson takes the ball around him, and from a tight angle, outside the box, whips it into an empty net.

"What a finish!" 😮‍💨 Evanilson makes it 3-0 to Bournemouth with a stunning goal https://t.co/hPMR78Z3cX

Joshua Zirkzee is likely to come on in a few seconds. He scored against Como and has looked a little more effective this season than last.

Martinez is penalised for tugging at Rayan.. It might be that Heaven and Martinez are just both having a hard time against an exceptional player.

Bruno Fernandes has been dropped for Manchester United’s crucial Premier League game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday.

Michael Carrick has taken the decision to drop the United captain to the bench in the wake of his public criticism on Wednesday following the shambolic 4-1 Champions League defeat to Como.

Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick’s tactics and has now been taken out of the starting XI.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Manchester United vs Bouremouth.

United enter Sunday’s clash against Bournemouth in the grip of a deepening crisis. Wednesday night’s dismal 4-1 Champions League defeat to debutants Como extended United’s’ winless run to seven matches across all competitions - their worst sequence since 2015.

With just one victory from their opening seven Premier League fixtures, United are enduring their worst start to a top-flight season since 1986-87. Head coach Michael Carrick, a multiple champion at Old Trafford during his playing days, finds his position under severe threat, with reports suggesting another defeat could seal his departure. While both of United’s wins this season have come at home, they remain winless in their last three at Old Trafford. On an individual level, Bryan Mbeumo has offered a rare bright spark, scoring four goals in seven league outings while Bruno Fernandes continues to search for form, and the captain’s recent outburst only makes the atmosphere more febrile.

In stark contrast, Bournemouth arrive in Manchester brimming with confidence. Marco Rose’s side have enjoyed a flawless start to their inaugural European campaign, sitting joint-top of the Europa League standings after a dominant 3-0 victory over Ruben Amorim’s ten-man AC Milan on Thursday. That result marked a third consecutive home win and clean sheet, with Bournemouth outscoring opponents 8-0 in that stretch. Midfielder Marcus Tavernier has been instrumental, leading the club’s scoring charts with five goals across 11 appearances.

Bournemouth will feel no trepidation visiting Old Trafford, having gone unbeaten in their last six Premier League meetings with United (two wins, four draws). With Carrick desperate for a stabilising result and Rose’s side riding high on European momentum, today’s fixture carries significant stakes for both clubs.

#1096. 'Ragebait' is the 2026 German Youth Word of the Year

Already named the 2025 Oxford Word of the Year, "rage bait" has also been widely adopted in German slang.

The 2026 Youth Word of the Year, "Ragebait," was announced on Saturday at the Frankfurt Book Fair by publisher PONS Langenscheidt.

The "Jugendwort des Jahres," or German Youth Word of the Year, is an annual campaign that documents the popularity of new slang expressions.

"Ragebait" (in English: rage bait) refers to social media content that is deliberately designed to make people angry, frustrated or morally outraged.

It aims to drive engagement, since the algorithms of platforms like Instagram, TikTok and X reward high-energy interaction. A post that generates a heated debate through angry comments, or that is widely shared due to the emotional reaction it provokes, counts as high engagement, which leads the platforms to push the content to more feeds.

"Ragebait" was on a shortlist of three words for the 2026 Youth Word of the Year, alongside "Peak" and "Crashout."

All three terms are borrowed from English, demonstrating once again the language's significant influence on German youth culture.

Around 1 million young people, aged 11 to 20, have voted since August 28 for their favorite term.

"Ragebait" obtained 36.5% of the votes, followed by 33.8% for "Peak" and 29.7% for "Crashout."

"The close result shows that all three terms have a firm place in the vocabulary of generations Z and Alpha," said Artur Raiser, marketing manager at PONS Langenscheidt, in a press statement. "'Ragebait' held a slight lead from the start," but only by a narrow margin throughout the voting period, he added.

"It remained an exciting race for us at the publishing house, too, until the very last moment," said Raiser

"Crashout" (used by young Germans as "crashout gehen," or "going crash out") originally comes from the English "to crash out," which traditionally means to fall asleep very quickly due to exhaustion.

But in newer internet slang, popularized on gaming and social media platforms, "crashing out" means having an intense emotional breakdown, losing control of one's temper or reacting with sudden, uncontrolled anger or stress. It is often used with a touch of humor, to emphasize that the reaction might be somewhat exaggerated.

As for the other shortlisted word, "Peak," it refers to something that is the absolute best. In German youth slang, it functions like an adjective: "That was peak football" or "that is peak comedy."

PONS Langenscheidt, a publishing company that specializes in language reference works, has been selecting the German Youth Word of the Year since 2008 — originally via a jury, and since 2020 through an online vote. Offensive, racist or discriminatory terms are not permitted. The multi-stage public nomination and voting process for next year's word will start in the summer of 2027.

"Das crazy" was selected last year, while "Aura" was the Youth Word of the Year 2024.

This article was originally written in German.
