#1054. How the brain protects itself from Parkinson’s disease

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Sarah DeWeerdt is a science journalist in Seattle, Washington.

The pianist’s hands are poised over the keys, his right hand trembles slightly. A drummer and bass player start up and, after a beat, the pianist joins in, both hands fluently producing the luscious, staccato rhythms of jazz.

The hands in this video from 2019 belong to Dutch musician René van Helsdingen, who had recently been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease. He uses strategies that reduce stress and emotion to help quiet the tremors that affect his right side and enable him to continue playing the music he loves, he explains in the video. “It’s my improvised solution.”

Improvisation is an apt metaphor for the ways in which many people with Parkinson’s learn to cope with the tremor, stiffness and movement difficulties that are characteristic of the neurodegenerative disease. Some use an external source of rhythm, such as a metronome, to overcome the tendency to ‘freeze up’ when walking or adopt a sideways crab-like gait. “I’m very inspired” by people’s creativity, says Rick Helmich, a neurologist at Radboud University in Nijmegen, the Netherlands, who has worked with van Helsdingen.

Other improvisations take place in the brain, beyond a person’s awareness, to preserve function in the face of Parkinson’s pathology. If scientists can understand them better and harness them more effectively, they might be able to slow the progression of Parkinson’s disease, delay its onset and even prevent it entirely, say researchers, such as Helmich.

The motor symptoms of Parkinson’s disease are caused by a loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra — part of a set of structures nestled deep in the brain known as the basal ganglia. But these symptoms do not emerge until at least 30% of those neurons are lost, and sometimes as many as 70%. Two people with a similar degree of neurodegeneration might have very different symptom severity. And some people’s condition worsens quickly, whereas others remain stable for years. Such observations have led most researchers and clinicians to agree that brain-based mechanisms of resilience must be important.

But for a long time, this area received little research attention because scientists focused instead on unravelling the pathology of the disease and on developing an effective treatment, called levodopa, that remedied the underlying dopamine loss. The awareness that the brain has ways of making up for the neurodegeneration in Parkinson’s hasn’t led to clinical advances, says Thilo van Eimeren, a specialist in brain imaging at the University of Cologne in Germany.

This area is now garnering more interest. It is a focus of a three-year, European Union-funded project launched in 2025, known as TRACE-PD, to track the mechanisms of disease progression and functional compensation in early stages of disease1.

The first task for the team from across Europe was to define its terms. That effort is more than mere semantics, says David Pedrosa, a neurologist at Marburg University in Germany and co-coordinator of the project. More clarity in the vocabulary that researchers use to talk about protective mechanisms will enable them to probe the underlying biology with greater precision, and design better targeted clinical trials to investigate how to bolster these processes, he explains.

The TRACE-PD consortium has defined resilience as an umbrella term that encompasses multiple protective mechanisms. One, called reserve, refers to neuronal resources built up across the lifespan that mitigate the effects of the disease. Another, called compensation, involves changes to neurons and brain networks that stabilize function in response to the disease.

The idea behind reserve makes intuitive sense: when a neurodegenerative process takes hold, individuals who have greater neural resources in a particular domain will take longer to decline to a point at which their impairment becomes obvious. Cognitive reserve has long been a focus of Alzheimer’s disease research. And over the past few years, studies of Parkinson’s have examined the idea of motor reserve.

Most such studies have defined individuals with high motor reserve as those with milder motor symptoms than their degree of dopamine-neuron loss would predict. A 2020 study by researchers in South Korea showed that people with newly diagnosed Parkinson’s and high motor reserve have greater connectivity between areas of the brain involved in movement, planning and control2. Greater connectivity in this network is also linked to a lower need for levodopa treatment.

“Individuals with higher motor reserve levels also show greater grey matter volume in motor-associated areas,” says Merle Hönig, a neuropsychologist at the University of Cologne. She and van Eimeren contributed to a study3 that also found that the gap in disease trajectory between individuals with high motor reserve and low motor reserve takes more than seven years to close, suggesting that assessing motor reserve early could help to determine prognosis.

But could motor reserve be the basis for interventions to alter the course of Parkinson’s? The same study showed an association between higher motor reserve and higher levels of physical activity in one cohort of people with the disease — a suggestive but circumstantial link. The team now has unpublished data that strengthen the case for a causal relationship by showing that people with higher lifetime levels of physical activity also have higher motor reserve. Exercise is known to slow progression during the early phases of Parkinson’s, but there is much about this connection that is poorly understood, says Patrick Santens, a neurologist at Ghent University in Belgium. “Nobody really knows what is the best,” he says. What type of exercise is beneficial, at what intensity and for which individuals?

Another question is the relationship between the different types of reserve. “We don’t know whether promoting, for example, cognitive reserve also helps to preserve motor reserve,” or vice versa, Hönig says. Research in this area might, therefore, have implications for multiple neurodegenerative diseases.

Research involving compensation goes back to at least the early 1990s. But over the past few years, Helmich says, the concept has been refined. Whereas greater activity in a brain area or network was once seen as evidence of compensation, scientists are now looking for a link between stronger hyperactivity and greater symptom reduction, for example.

This approach has enabled researchers to zero in on the neural substrate of compensation. Helmich and his team have shown that the main brain areas involved are the parietal cortex and the premotor cortex. The less affected parts of the basal ganglia also contribute4.

Another group have investigated brain activity in people with dopamine-neuron loss on both sides of the brain, but symptoms on only one side of the body. The researchers identified several compensatory mechanisms in the brain hemisphere that controls the unaffected side of the body, including increased plasticity in motor networks5.

Helmich and his team have also shown6 that, over the course of two years, “the speed of progression relates to the collapse of compensatory mechanisms”, he says. The researchers have unpublished data from a separate cohort showing that people who have mutations in the gene encoding the enzyme glucocerebrosidase, long known to increase the risk of Parkinson’s, have reduced potential for compensation. Such studies place the loss of compensation at the centre of disease progression.

Researchers are now beginning to investigate how to intervene to stimulate compensatory mechanisms. Helmich and his team identified an ‘anti tremor network’ that comes online when a tremor reduces in intensity and consists of areas of the cortex involved in attention and in interpreting bodily sensations7. He is testing whether an intervention involving mindfulness training and meditation can help people to activate this network and control the tremor.

Stimulating compensatory mechanisms might also involve non-invasive brain stimulation — Helmich plans to launch a study later this year using transcranial ultrasound to activate the less affected parts of the basal ganglia to find out. Meanwhile, Pedrosa is investigating how to use advancing knowledge of compensation to improve deep-brain stimulation, a treatment in which electrodes are implanted in the brain to send electrical signals to areas involved in motor control.

Further research will be needed to help refine and guide these approaches, says Josefine Waldthaler, a neuroimaging specialist at the Karolinska Institute in Sweden. “We know where to look” for compensation in the cerebral cortex, Waldthaler says, but not the particular patterns of brain activity that define it, and therefore what brain frequency interventions need to stimulate.

Magnetoencephalography, an imaging method that is Waldthaler’s specialty, could fill in some of those details. And that’s where TRACE-PD comes in. The effort brings together researchers who use different approaches to investigate various aspects of resilience. Rather than collect new data, the idea is to share existing data sets and analytical methods. This will help the consortium to tease apart the mechanisms of compensation and reserve, validate definitions and refine applications, Pedrosa says. What the researchers find could have broader relevance as well. “The cool thing about the idea of compensation and reserve is that it’s not a Parkinson’s specific idea,” says Pedrosa. He contends that the group’s insights might shed light on other neurodegenerative conditions, such as Alzheimer’s disease, as well as on strategies for healthy ageing.

And although TRACE-PD focuses on early Parkinson’s, the processes it looks at might still be harnessed later in the disease. In May, van Helsdingen performed with his trio in Italy. In a video of the concert, his symptoms seem to have worsened since 2019. He rocks rhythmically back and forth as he plays, and at one point crosses his left wrist over his right to execute a particularly tricky sequence of notes on the upper keys with his less-affected left hand. But the result is syncopated, at times cheerful, music that makes it clear he’s still improvising.

#1052. Suzuki howler costs Aston Villa crucial points

Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki went from being serenaded with a chorus of “world’s No 1” to making a bizarre blunder that denied Unai Emery’s side a third successive Premier League victory.

The Villa manager, however, preferred to focus on a string of important saves from Suzuki rather than the uncharacteristic mistake that allowed Fulham to collect a deserved point.

It all went wrong for the hosts just after the hour mark in a match where Fulham provided more than a few scares before finding the net in unexpected fashion.

Alex Iwobi, who had been denied superbly by a Suzuki save just moments earlier, swung in a corner. It was right on top of the Villa goalkeeper, who tried to keep it out but only succeeded in fumbling it over the line. A frantic attempt to gather the ball was in vain and goal-line technology confirmed the goal stood.

Zion Suzuki drops Alex Iwobi's corner and Fulham are level! 🫨 https://t.co/KwLFMRpKqk

Suzuki appeared to have been put off by the presence of Fulham’s Shea Charles, but Emery refused to single out the player for criticism.

“I prefer to speak about the saves that he made,” the Villa manager said. “This is part of football. I think he played fantastically and he is doing a lot of saves so he can make one mistake. It is part of football. We can be mature about this.

“I still want to see consistency. Over the last five Premier League matches, we are winning three and drawing two. It’s not bad but with our poor start it’s not enough.

“We have to change our mind quickly for Tuesday against Barcelona. We want to test ourselves at this level.”

Villa go to the Nou Camp with a 100 per cent Champions League record to their name this season. But they will need to improve on Saturday evening’s performance to get a result in Spain.

As well as Suzuki’s error, a 14th-minute penalty miss from John McGinn also proved costly.

It was awarded after Leon Goretzka, making his full league debut for Villa, saw his header hit Sander Berge’s raised hand. Nobody appealed at the time but referee Sam Barrott was sent to the touchline monitor by VAR to review the incident and gave the spot-kick.

McGinn’s attempt, however, hit the crossbar and the chance to take an early lead went begging. The Villa captain seemed a strange choice to take the spot-kick as he has only ever scored one career penalty, but Emery defended the choice, saying: “We analysed the penalty takers in the squad and it was McGinn here.”

Penalty MISSED! John McGinn hits the bar 💥 https://t.co/2kBYkYA2BY

Nicolas Jackson was on hand to ease Villa’s nerves before the break, though. the Villa manager had said before the game that the striker’s goalscoring capability meant he was capable of matching the likes of Harry Kane. His assessment was backed up by Jackson scoring the opening goal, after 40 minutes, which summed up the striker in one moment of pure power combined with agility.

Collecting Johan Manzambi’s superbly weighted pass, Jackson forced his way past two defenders before sliding in the goal that put Villa ahead.

Emery’s touchline celebrations said it all as the Senegal forward continues to flourish under the man who knew how to get the best out of him at Villarreal.

Nicolas Jackson scores his fifth league goal in five games! 🔥 https://t.co/W0xmFtW1Gt

Suzuki has also flourished under Emery and he kept Villa in the game with some superb saves.

When Antonee Robinson crossed for Gonzalo Garcia, his step over allowed Oscar Bobb in for what looked like his second goal in successive games. But Suzuki pulled off a stunning fingertip save. That had Villa supporters singing: “Zion Suzuki, the world’s No 1”.

Robinson put in another cross and Suzuki got a touch that was enough to make Garcia put his shot wide. Villa were living dangerously and the Japanese goalkeeper made another outstanding stop to keep out Iwobi’s header. But then it all went wrong for Suzuki when he fumbled Iwobi’s corner.

That allowed Fulham’s recent revival under manager, Alvaro Arbeloa, to continue – they now have seven points from their past three games.

“We spoke at half-time about what we had to do,” Arbeloa said. “If you want to win a game you have to fight and I think we have to believe in our way, we’ve shown we can beat anyone in the way that we play but we have to be aggressive.

“We created so many chances and at the end it’s one point in a difficult stadium. I’m so happy with the second half because of the way we played, this is the team that we want to be.”

"This is the first time I've seen him that little bit confused" Rob Green analyses Zion Suzuki's error that lead to Fulham's equaliser 🔍 https://t.co/B3HCivNpwz

"I don't think he gets the flowers he deserves" 💐 Jamie Redknapp is a fan of Calvin Bassey 🫡 https://t.co/R9uravAzRU

“We started the game well. Fulham are a good side, not easy to win [against] but we came in front. We did well but in the second half we gave them more time on the ball. They have good players and they can make chances. We were unlucky with the goal but we tried to keep fighting. It is important not to lose these games.”

On Zion Suzuki’s mistake for Fulham’s equaliser:

“It is frustrating because we do not want to concede goals but it can happen to everyone. Zion is a great guy, great goalkeeper. He will learn from it. We will support him and go again.”

"We should have got more" Calvin Bassey believes Fulham should have came away with three points against Aston Villa ⤵️ https://t.co/pMTMtc4zjS

The final whistle is blown at Villa Park and both sides take a point from the game. Aston Villa took the lead through Jackson but Suzuki’s blunder gifted Fulham the equalising goal. Fulham were fully deserving of a point this evening despite falling behind.

Aston Villa have a free-kick inside the Fulham half late on as Palacios needlessly brings down Jackson. This will go into the Fulham penalty area. Aston Villa take it short before Buendia clips it in. Barkley attempts an overhead kick and his effort is blocked. There are appeals for handball but even if it did hit Berge’s arm he was right next to Barkley. It does hit the arm but that is never a penalty.

Garnacho has a shot blocked from just inside the Fulham penalty area.

Torres has already wasted one good chance with his head from eight yards out and there is another. That probably should have found the corner of the net.

Late double change for Fulham as Muniz and Larsson enter the fray.

Aston Villa are also making a late alteration as Garnacho replaces McGinn.

Chance for Aston Villa. Cash clips in a delivery from the right and Torres has a good chance from eight yards out but the Spaniard’s header goes wide.

This game is there for the taking for both sides, although Fulham have been much the better side since the break and currently look more likely to get the winner.

Changes for both sides. For Aston Villa, they bring Barkley on for Kamara.

Fulham meanwhile bring on Palacios and Tete.

Cairney has not been on the pitch long but he is already into the book for cynically bringing down Mbaye.

Cash fouls King and is punished with a yellow card. That is already Cash’s fifth yellow card of the campaign, which means he will miss their trip to Manchester United next weekend.

Fulham are carving Aston Villa open. Bobb drives down their right wing before cutting inside. As he approaches the Aston Villa penalty area, he plays it out to his left to pick out Iwobi in space. Iwobi could hit it first time but instead cuts back onto his right, which allows Cash to block the shot but it does spin behind for a corner.

Before that is taken, Cairney replaces Iwobi. The corner comes to nothing.

Fulham have not made any substitutions yet but based on the way they are playing, they really do not need to right now, unless anyone is exhausted.

You can hear the groans inside Villa Park as the home fans grow frustrated with their side’s performance since the break.

Fulham deserved that equaliser and have been the better side in this game, especially since the break. It does feel like this game is for the taking for Alvaro Arbeloa’s men heading into the final 20 minutes.

Unai Emery has unsurprisingly made a triple change as Mbaye, Buendia and Gomes come on.

The Aston Villa goalkeeper has been outstanding tonight but that is a huge error. The corner is swung in by Iwobi from the left and Suzuki should simply catch it. He backpedals towards his own line and ends up dropping it. By the time he re-gathers, the ball has crossed the line and Fulham have an equaliser that they deserve.

Zion Suzuki drops Alex Iwobi's corner and Fulham are level! 🫨 https://t.co/KwLFMRpKqk

An important save from Leno. Maatsen’s volley from the edge of the box takes a deflection off his teammate Torres, forcing Leno into a good reflex save. Had that gone in, it may have been curtains for Fulham.

The chances are piling up for Fulham but they still have not been able to take advantage of any of them. First Bobb has a shot inside the box blocked before Charles curls off target from the edge of the box.

Suzuki does brilliantly to stick out a hand and the ball flies into the sliding Garcia, ricocheting off the forward and going wide. Suzuki has been crucial for Aston Villa tonight; without him having a good game thus far, Fulham may have scored a couple of times.

Fulham almost took the lead when Antonee Robinson broke clear and crossed for Gonzalo Garcia, his step over allowed Oscar Bobb in for what looked like his second goal in successive games.

Bassey is into the book late on in the half for a foul on Kamara.

The first half is then brought to an end moments later and Aston Villa lead 1-0 at the break thanks to Jackson’s goal. McGinn did miss a penalty for the hosts whilst Fulham have failed to take a few good chances.

Fulham have had some chances in the first half but have not been able to take advantage of any of them. King has the ball on the right side of the box and tries to pick out Garcia at the far post but there is just slightly too much on the cross.

King has a chance to equalise for Fulham but Suzuki is quick off his line to snuff out the danger. That is two big moments from Suzuki to prevent Fulham from scoring.

There will be four added minutes at the end of this first half.

Fulham wasted a fifth minute chance and may regret it. Gonzalo Garcia crossed for Alex Iwobi who sent his shot over the bar.

Villa awarded a penalty in the 14th after a VAR review when Leon Goretzka’s header hit Sande Berge’s raised hand. No-one appealed at the time but referee Sam Barrott was sent to the touchline monitor to review the incident and gave the spot-kick.

But Villa captain John McGinn’s shot hit the crossbar and bounced out again. It was a mystery as to why he took it with Nicolas Jackson available, but Villa are the team on top here.

Fulham are currently having to do a lot of defending, especially negotiating set-pieces. Affengruber is on hand this time to head away McGinn’s corner from the right.

McGinn steps up but his effort smashes into the bar. Leno dived the wrong way but there is too much power and loft on that effort. A massive missed opportunity for Aston Villa and the most relieved man inside Villa Park right now will be Berge.

Penalty MISSED! John McGinn hits the bar 💥 https://t.co/2kBYkYA2BY

Berge is pretty close to Goretzka but there is no reason why his arm is above his head like that.

It is adjudged to have been a handball from Berge and Aston Villa are awarded the penalty. That feels like the only decision the referee could come to in all honesty.

Another McGinn corner from the right is met by Goretzka. This time, the German gets his header on target but it is easily saved by his compatriot Leno.

There is a VAR check for a possible penalty. Is there a handball from Berge in there immediately after Goretzka got his head on the ball? It appears that it did strike Berge’s hand and the referee is sent to the screen. We know how this normally goes...

Alysson goes down inside the Fulham box, wanting a penalty, but he is not going to get that.

Aston Villa do have a corner though, which McGinn delivers. His corner is met by Goretzka, who cannot keep his header down and it goes off target.

That is a big early chance for Fulham which Iwobi wastes. Bobb steals possession deep inside his own half and drives forward into the Aston Villa half. He then finds Garcia to his right, who delivers a cross from the right side of the box. There is a nick off Lindelof and comes to Iwobi near the penalty spot but he blazes his effort into the stands. At the very least, Iwobi should be hitting the target.

Is that an example of the time of the game contributing to a decision? Goretzka is pulled back by Garcia, who avoids a yellow card. Had that not been inside the first few minutes of the game, it would not have been a surprise to have seen a yellow card.

After the Remembrance tribute is impeccably observed by those inside Villa Park, we are under way in the final Premier League game of the day.

With this being Aston Villa’s last home league game before Remembrance Sunday, Villa Park pauses to pay tribute to remember the fallen. Wreaths are laid in the middle of the centre circle before The Last Post is played.

As the pyrotechnics go off, both sides emerge from the tunnel and we are moments away from kick-off at Villa Park. Here is a reminder of how the two sides line up this evening:

Aston Villa: Suzuki, Cash, Lindelof, Torres, Maatsen, Kamara, Goretzka, Alysson, Manzambi, McGinn, Jackson.Substitutes: Bizot, Harwood-Bellis, Mings, Barkley, Buendia, Garnacho, Mbaye, Joao Gomes, Madjo.

Fulham: Leno, Castagne, Affengruber, Bassey, Robinson, Berge, Charles, Bobb, King, Iwobi, Garcia.Substitutes: Lecomte, Tete, Andersen, Palacios, Rodrigo Muniz, Cairney, Kevin, Larsson, Angel.

Games: 18Aston Villa wins: 12Fulham wins: 1Draws: 5

Zion Suzuki had big gloves to fill this summer after the sale of Emiliano Martínez but already appears one of the Premier League signings of the summer.

Aston Villa’s new No 1 epitomises the vibrant energy of Unai Emery’s revamped squad and is a goalkeeper perfectly suited to the modern game.

The Japanese international is Villa’s own version of former Manchester City goalkeeper Ederson, who revolutionised English football with a vast range of passing from his own penalty area.

Of all the daft statements to have come out of Aston Villa – and I am including Doug Ellis’s frequent claims that he invented the bicycle kick – it is hard to think of anything as absurd as suing a pundit for speaking the truth.

Jamie Carragher’s common-sense declaration that Villa manager Unai Emery might consider a move to Manchester United – because it is a bigger club – has apparently inflicted such a deep wound to the self-esteem of Nassef Sawiris, the chairman, that he has initiated a legal complaint.

Sawiris’s short statement, which he published on social media on Friday night, consisted of 37 ill-chosen words. It started by accusing Carragher of “unacceptable insults to the club and its fans”, then concluded with the vainglorious declaration that “Aston Villa will not allow anyone to stop our ascension in English and European football”.

ASTON VILLA XI TO FACE FULHAM: Suzuki, Cash, Lindelof, Torres, Maatsen, Kamara, Goretzka, Alysson, Manzambi, McGinn, Jackson

Subs: Bizot, Harwood-Bellis, Mings, Barkley, Buendia, Garnacho, Mbaye, Joao Gomes, Madjo

FULHAM XI TO FACE ASTON VILLA: Leno, Castagne, Affengruber, Bassey, Robinson, Berge, Charles, Bobb, King, Iwobi, Garcia

Subs: Lecomte, Tete, Andersen, Palacios, Rodrigo Muniz, Cairney, Kevin, Larsson, Angel

Aston Villa manager, Unai Emery, is giving a full Premier League debut to Germany midfielder Leon Goretzka against Fulham this evening.

The 31-year-old joined Villa on a free transfer in the summer, but a knee injury prevented him from making an appearance off the bench until this month’s Champions League tie against Fenerbahce.

Asked what role Goretzka would have with Villa, Emery deadpanned: “The first one is to be available to play.”

Emery had also made a cryptic remark about Nicolas Jackson and Johann Manzambi in his Friday press conference. The suggestion was that they had been merely rested for Wednesday’s Carabao Cup defeat at Bournemouth.

But the Spaniard said: “For different reasons, not only rest.”

Whatever he meant is unclear, but both start for Villa tonight.

Fulham have won their last two league games – against Hull and Coventry.

Manager, Alvaro Arbeloa, has made one change with Sander Berge replacing Hugo Larsson in midfield.

Villa are aiming to win three successive league games for the first time in this calendar year. The omens are good as they’ve beaten Fulham in their last seven league meetings at Villa Park.

Tonight sees a battle between two Spaniards at Villa Park as Aston Villa host Fulham. Both sides are looking to bounce back from disappointing midweeks having been knocked out of the League Cup; Aston Villa lost 3-0 at Bournemouth, while Fulham fell to a 1-0 defeat at home against Crystal Palace.

After a slow start to the season in the league, Aston Villa’s form has picked up, which includes handing Manchester City their first defeat of the season a week ago. After this evening, Aston Villa have games against Barcelona and Manchester United before the international break but Unai Emery has insisted his full focus is on this game.

“If we are thinking after the match against Fulham, then we are making a mistake and we are completely wrong,” Emery said. “We are prioritising the Premier League, and this is the message. To keep our consistency and demands means that each match is a test.”

Having failed to win any of their first six league games, Fulham have now won back-to-back Premier League games, with consecutive 1-0 wins over Hull and Coventry, which has lifted them out of the relegation zone.

“It [managing in England] is a very tough challenge but I am so happy to be here,” Alvaro Arbeloa said. “I am where I want to be and I am really enjoying my days. I want to win games and I think we are performing well but we need to improve.

“They [Aston Villa] are very compact, they defend so well and even with the ball they know what they have to do. And they have top players, and when you have a top coach with top players, normally you have a top team. I think right now he [Unai Emery] is one of the best coaches in the world. He is very, very good, he improves everything every year. It does not matter where he is coaching, he is doing an amazing job, and for me also it is a very good challenge to face him.”

In the two league meetings between these sides last season, it was one win apiece; Aston Villa won this fixture 3-1 just over a year ago before Fulham won 1-0 at Craven Cottage back in April. Team news from Villa Park to follow shortly.

#1051. Trump's diesel deal with Russia is unlikely to significantly lower global fuel prices despite expectations of rapid relief

As the world's largest diesel exporter, the US benefits from high prices. At home, however, consumers are feeling the strain of rising living costs. Why Donald Trump's deal with Russia is unlikely to change that.

With or without a deal with Russia, diesel prices on global markets are unlikely to fall significantly anytime soon.

That is the assessment of experts interviewed by DW regarding the latest fuel-supply agreement between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

"The main reason for high diesel prices is the war in Iran and the simultaneous disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait," said Samina Sultan, a foreign trade expert at the German Economic Institute (IW) in Cologne.

The situation has led to production outages and made fuel shipments "more expensive, less secure and more difficult," she said.

Trump's deal with Russia also has an additional geopolitical dimension, Sultan said: "It causes the wars in Ukraine and Iran to become completely intertwined."

Things are looking up, though. Roughly 13.5 million barrels of crude oil are once again flowing through the Strait of Hormuz a day, according to shipping and commodities analytics firm Kpler.

But for refined products such as diesel, volumes remain far lower at around 677,000 barrels per day, compared with 3.6 million barrels before the war.

Carsten Fritsch, a commodities analyst at Commerzbank, also attributes the price increases to the wars.

"If nothing changes in Ukraine and the Middle East, I see very few ways to resolve these supply bottlenecks," he said.

In a social media post on October 9, Trump announced that he would temporarily suspend some sanctions on Russia and begin importing Russian diesel.

He wrote "diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" in a mix of lowercase and all caps.

Russia confirmed the arrangement. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agency TASS on October 13 that supplying diesel fuel was "in the interests of Russia, the United States and global energy markets."

Diesel prices in the US and many EU countries have risen sharply over the past 12 months.

According to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), prices in the US have climbed by about 60% and now stand at $6.30 per gallon, equivalent to $1.66 (or €1.49) per liter of diesel.

But even if Russia were able to flood global markets with cheap diesel, prices would not fall nearly as much as they recently rose, something all of the experts contacted by DW agree on.

Many refineries around the Gulf region have suffered disruptions or damage, while transporting fuel via shadow fleets and securing insurance remains costly, cumbersome and risky.

Another key shift is that Russia is no longer the world's largest diesel exporter. In fact, it is facing its own fuel shortages at home.

The US is now the world's biggest diesel exporter. In 2025, it exported an average of 1.26 million barrels of diesel per day, accounting for roughly 15.4% of global diesel exports.

At the same time, Russia fell to second place with a 9.5% share, and that was before major Ukrainian drone attacks on its refineries.

Besides the new US-Russia diesel agreement, Trump also recently floated the idea of US diesel export restrictions. But the idea was abandoned because it could lead to even higher diesel prices in the country, according to Samina Sultan.

"There simply is not enough diesel storage capacity in the United States," Sultan said. "Production would have to be reduced, and then prices would rise again."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

If the US were to impose export restrictions on diesel, buyers in Latin America and the European Union would be hit particularly hard. Since Russia invaded Ukraine, EU countries have increasingly imported diesel from the US instead of Russia because of sanctions.

"An export ban merely redistributes the shortage; it does not solve it," said ING chief economist Carsten Brzeski.

"Global prices would continue to rise, while refineries would scale back production as margins shrink," he added.

Export restrictions aside, few people consider that the US-Russia diesel deal will have any big impact.

According to calculations by the platform The World Data, the promised shipment of 2.2 million barrels of diesel from Russia would not even cover a single day's US diesel demand of roughly 4 million barrels.

Even if all of the diesel volumes announced by Trump were combined, totaling 35.8 million barrels, they would only cover about nine days of US domestic demand.

"I CANNOT OVERSTATE HOW MUCH OF A NOTHING BURGER THIS IS," Canadian oil market analyst Rory Johnston wrote in an all-caps post on X shortly after the announcement.

Russia would normally export almost 10 times that volume if its refinery fleet was not being targeted by Ukrainian drone attacks, he added.

Canada also supplies diesel to the United States. Roughly 80% of all US diesel imports come from its northern neighbor.

Given Trump's verbal attacks on Canada and the ongoing trade dispute, analysts view the prospect of Canada supplying significantly more diesel to the US as highly unlikely.

This piece was originally published in German.

#1049. AI agents enter the ‘wet lab’

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

James Zou is in the Department of Biomedical Data Science, Stanford University, Stanford, California 94305, USA.

Artificial intelligence has been tremendously useful in science, but, most of the time, it is used for computational work, such as analysing data, making predictions and scouring literature. Carrying out ‘wet laboratory’ experiments — which involve handling liquids, biological material and chemicals — is another matter. An AI system might design a promising biologically active molecule in minutes, but testing it can take weeks or months and requires extensive human effort. In a paper published in Nature, Wu et al.1 introduce AutoDNA, a lab in which AI agents plan and conduct molecular-biology experiments involving DNA, with relatively little human intervention. The work shows how AI systems can begin to close the gap between proposing an experiment and doing it.

#1048. Manchester City, the UAE and the UK's PM in a political tangle

Nearly 20 years after arriving in England, Manchester City's UAE owners could exit amid cheating charges. That would pose a challenge for a city — and prime minister — closely tied to Abu Dhabi.

Defiance was the word that stood out as Manchester City returned home for the first time since they were found guilty of 114 financial charges by the Premier League in a case that's made headlines around the world.

City showed a measure of it on the pitch, even as they lost 4-2 to holders, Qatari-owned Paris Saint-Germain, in the Champions League group stages on Wednesday.

Among the home fanbase at the Etihad Stadium, DW found universal support for City's Abu Dhabi owners — headed by Sheikh Mansour, who is also UAE's vice president and deputy prime minister.

"I'm all in with the ownership now," said local fan Matt. "If we end up back in League Two [fourth tier], so be it. We've got 15 years of memories we wouldn't have otherwise and to me it's just an accounting line on a spreadsheet really."

The stadium name itself is a reminder of the takeover that changed this club, and its part of Manchester, in 2008. The national airline of the UAE, Etihad's inflated sponsorship of City is among the key planks of the case against them, while many buildings and businesses around the stadium bear the brand. It's a stadium that's also seen plenty of success of late.

"We've seen things other fans will never see," added fellow City fan Josh. "I think people have got to consider how many people this club has given great memories to, how many people's lives have been changed by it, myself included....you've got to be grateful for that."

Though many in sky blue shared those sentiments, most outside the club now view the trophies won in the relevant period as tarnished. On top of that, critics point to City's reticence in providing evidence in their case, the long-documented human rights abuses in UAE and the often dismissive tone with which the owners have dealt with being found guilty of charges they have now appealed.

But those City fans appear to have one powerful ally in British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. Though he has since sought to tone down his position on Mansour and co. somewhat, the former mayor of Greater Manchester said he "would be really concerned to lose them," after the verdict was announced in late September. "They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester," he added.

While Burnham has since denied being close to City's ownership, even as City were playing on Wednesday, The Guardian reported a club representative was invited on a government-backed trade delegation to India this week by Burnham's successor as Manchester mayor, Bev Craig.

Earlier the same day, Burnham was forced to confirm he had two additional dinners with the club chair, Khaldoon Al Mubarak, at the Etihad Stadium, having previously declared those only as matchday hospitality. It has become a serious domestic issue for the man who replaced Keir Starmer in July.

What is clear is that Burnham welcomed Abu Dhabi investment during his time in charge of the northwestern city. This came mainly in the form of residential and commercial buildings as well as libraries and sports centers, all popping up in previously run-down areas in and around the stadium.

Georgina Blakeley, a Professor at the University of Huddersfield who wrote a book called "The regeneration of east Manchester," told DW that UAE investment has transformed swathes of the city.

"One of the prime drivers for building this partnership with the Abu Dhabi United Group [a private equity arm of the state mostly concerned with the football club] was that at that point in time, 2014, there was no other private investor willing to invest at the scale that the council wanted. And to do so in a way that created a build-to-rent market," she said.

The UAE investment in Manchester, accelerated by the Manchester Life Partnership with the city's council signed in 2014, has been a key defense for the City owners and fans when faced with sportswashing allegations in the past. And while Blakeley believes councils in the UK are often forced to seek foreign investment, there has been some pushback on how east Manchester has changed.

"A lot of people would be critical of some of the developments in [the districts of] Ancoats and New Islington and say that it's gentrified the area and there are some tensions between newer populations coming in and living in the more expensive flats and those already there. I think there's some truth to it. But I also think there's some truth to the fact that people forget really, really quickly that if you go back to just the 1990s, Ancoats was a no-go area," she said.

While profit for both council and state have certainly been a driver of the partnership, Blakeley thinks that forging greater links to the community could be something City's owners see "as a beneficial side effect."

After 18 years in the club and city, the UAE are deeply embedded in this part of Manchester. With political ties between the UK and UAE now reportedly strained as a result of the charges, there are suggestions that City's owners will try to sell the club. They may also be forced to do so, with sanctions still to be decided pending City's appeal.

There is no such trouble at PSG, who look capable of winning a third straight Champions League powered by their own Gulf-State coffers.

What is clear is that state-owned football clubs can become successful fast in a free market, as the Premier League was when the UAE owners arrived. Deep pockets, strong contacts at the top tables of the sport and canny strategies to integrate with the local area can be a heady mix.

It's certainly one that's proved intoxicating to City's fans, who brush off secret second contracts, sham sponsorship and unreliable witnesses with a loyalty built on success, community and investment. Judging by the mood in Manchester on Wednesday, no sanctions are going to change that.

#1047. Arsenal nous frustrates Liverpool as 14-year Anfield hoodoo ends with statement win

It is clear and obvious that Arsenal will be the team to beat in the Premier League title race, especially given that we do not yet know the fate of faltering Manchester City and their looming punishment.

A statement victory against Liverpool, their first in the league at Anfield since 2012, took Arsenal back to the top. And who would bet against them staying there and retaining their title?

Few would when they defend and manage a game – and it was game management in every sense – like this. From the formidable to the cynical – that was the statement. Against the Scousers, Arsenal had the nous.

“The mission was something we didn’t complete in 14 years,” Mikel Arteta said, having famously – in an Amazon documentary series – played You’ll Never Walk Alone to his players as they walked out to train to try and overcome a perceived mental block.

“There are reasons for that. Some of it psychological, some of it moments we did not nail on the pitch,” the Arsenal manager added of the winless run.

The result means that the north Londoners have already now won away at Villa Park, the Stadium of Light, the City Ground and Anfield. Stadiums where they dropped points last season. And that feels ominous.

A win would maybe have thrust Liverpool into the title race. Instead, under Andoni Iraola, and with an evolving young team – with promising 19-year-old midfielder Trey Nyoni handed his league debut – they are already nine points behind after just nine matches.

It is also clear, however, that they could have prevented this defeat having somehow been denied a first-half penalty after Alexander Isak’s shirt was blatantly pulled by Jurrien Timber as the striker tried to head home a cross.

Referee Andy Madley may have missed it, but what was the excuse of Stuart Attwell, the VAR? It was a stunningly poor decision – another bad day for Pro Ref and the use of technology.

It might be argued that Timber did not pull hard enough to prevent Isak from reaching the ball. But the defender grabbed the shirt and continued to hold it for a long time. It had to be a penalty. Little wonder Iraola said Isak should dive next time. Who can blame him?

What is also clear and obvious is that, once again, Arsenal’s resilience, defensive determination and appetite for toughing it out will be their greatest weapons. They are certainly, under Arteta, not here to win friends – just to win matches and trophies.

“That defensive line, that togetherness we have is undefeated. It’s something I have never seen before,” Declan Rice, who was also a stand-out performer and delivered a fine assist for the winner, said.

Arsenal’s version of the Yellow Wall was, indeed, hugely impressive – it is now six clean sheets from their nine league games and, despite all their pressure, Liverpool did not have a shot on target. That has never happened in the Premier League since such statistics started to be compiled in 2003 (422 games ago).

“That’s incredible. It did not feel like it on the pitch. Again, it’s the commitment of every single player,” Arteta said. And that was indisputable.

Even the expected second-half momentum, the expected surge of attack after attack as Liverpool faced the Kop, crashed on Arsenal’s back line. The visitors were so well-drilled that they stifled space – they refused to crumble.

Arsenal put their bodies on the line with blocks and tackles and a bit of time-wasting. There were dark arts, especially from both centre-halves with Gabriel going unpunished after claiming he was struck in the face by Isak early on – VAR anyone? – and the otherwise outstanding Ezri Konsa throwing himself to the ground after minimal contact from the Liverpool centre-forward.

In fairness there was also a bit of that from an increasingly frustrated Liverpool with Alexis Mac Allister going down after touching heads with Noni Madueke, having already tried to provoke Martin Odegaard with a hand to the head when the Arsenal captain was on the turf. That was not good from Mac Allister either.

And the only goal? Again, more frustration for Liverpool. It was well-constructed from Arsenal, but only after Alisson Becker’s loose goal kick, aimed towards Jérémy Jacquet, who was slow to react, was intercepted by Odegaard with Bruno Guimarães poking the ball to the right, where it was collected by Madueke.

There was an overlap by Rice and his low centre was precise and dangerous across the face of the six-yard area, with Virgil van Dijk unsure what to do. It ran beyond the far post where Kai Havertz side-footed home.

Every manager has different solutions and a different approach and Andoni’s is very clear. We expect a different game to that one [last year when Arne Slot’s side won 1-0]. It is a team that is very vertical with a real capacity to create chaos from almost all situations. They’re very good in the high press with great individuals.

[On selection] We have had issues this week with ankles and other things and had to be smart how we manage the minutes today to have players for the minutes they are available for. The conditions and the context force you to make certain decisions [on Tzolis coming straight back in after a month out].

We can’t wait. This is the kind of opportunity, challenge, mission you want to come to Anfield for.

There will be a commemoration of the fallen and pledge to care for the living before the match.

🟡 𝗧𝗘𝗔𝗠𝙉𝙀𝙒𝙎 🔵 Your Gunners, representing north London 👊 🤝 @deel

Here is a question I did not think I would be asking at any stage this season: will Liverpool win the Premier League?

It would be premature to describe this Sunday’s Anfield fixture as a title duel. Arsenal are better equipped to defend their crown, while Liverpool are a work in progress.

Whatever the outcome this weekend, Arsenal will leave Merseyside as the overwhelming favourites to claim back-to-back titles. They have a six-point lead over Liverpool. Should that extend to nine, Andoni Iraola’s primary objective coming into this season will remain unchanged; qualifying for the Champions League will represent a promising start to his reign.

What makes this weekend more significant is the champions will find a different Anfield to that which ended last season in such a downbeat mood, and came into this one uncertain of what was in store.

The discussion about what is achievable for Liverpool in the coming months is evolving by the week, the team bubbling along slightly under the radar.

There are several reasons why there are those who believe Iraola’s side might push Arsenal closer than anticipated.

Good afternoon and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Liverpool, who start the game in fifth with 15 points, and Arsenal, six points in front of them in second place. Anfield, that glorious night in May 1989 excepted, has not been the happiest of hunting grounds for Arsenal and though their record there recently – three draws in the last four visits – has perked up, they have gone 13 seasons without a victory, so long ago, in fact, that Mikel Arteta was in the side that celebrated Lukas Podolski  and Santo Cazorla earning them a 2-0 win.

Having already lost within the perimeter of the historic county of Lancashire this week, when knocked out of the Carabao Cup on penalties by League Two Fleetwood Town, the champions will be keen to end that barren streak and go into the 4.30pm kick-off on the back of three successive league victories following their defeat by Brighton. Points today, one or three, will put them ahead of Manchester City at the top of the table while victory for Liverpool would allow them to overtake Chelsea and move one point behind Brighton, the team they beat last week with the kind of performance that inspired talk of a credible title campaign.

For the visitors Max Dowman is suspended after his red card at Highbury and Bukayo Saka and William Saliba are sidelined for at least another three weeks with injury. #1045. 'Most difficult days of my life' for Owono after De Miguel death

Fans pay respects to Tenerife's De Miguel

FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono says he is experiencing "the most difficult days of my life" after the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.

Tenerife player De Miguel, 30, died after suffering a serious injury in a collision with Owono during a Spanish second division match on Monday.

The world of football has paid tribute to De Miguel, a father-of-one who joined Tenerife in summer 2025, with a minute's silence being held at all games in European competition this week.

Owono's club issued a statement on the goalkeeper's behalf on Wednesday, explaining the 25-year-old "wishes to share a few words personally".

"These are the most difficult days of my life," Owono says in the statement.

"I struggle to find the words, and it is very hard for me to come to terms with what has happened.

"I feel enormous pain over the loss of Jesus. I think of him, his family, and everyone who loved him.

"I know there will be many issues to address, and I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect. But right now, honestly, I cannot think about anything other than Jesus and the pain we are all experiencing.

Earlier on Wednesday, FC Andorra team-mate Lautaro Spatz defended Owono and said he "would never intentionally hurt anyone" and had been "deeply affected" by De Miguel's death.

Writing on social media, centre-back Spatz said Owono was devastated.

Spatz paid tribute to De Miguel, then said of Owono: "Those of us who know him know the kind of person he is, how much he is suffering at this moment and that he would never intentionally hurt anyone.

"In football, unfortunate incidents can happen but no-one could imagine that one of them might end with such tragic consequences."

Players from FC Andorra held a minute's silence before a voluntary training session on Wednesday. Owono was not at the session.

Football world mourns Tenerife striker De Miguel

Tenerife and Andorra were drawing 2-2 seven minutes into stoppage time on Monday when the incident occurred.

Owono ran towards the centre circle to clear a long ball when his knee appeared to collide with De Miguel.

The striker lay motionless on the pitch as medical staff treated him, before he was taken by ambulance from Tenerife's Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez to hospital.

Owono was sent off and the match was abandoned.

The goalkeeper, who had over 30,000 followers on Instagram on Tuesday morning, has since deactivated his account.

Police in Spain opened a routine investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter following De Miguel's death.

Under Spanish law, any death that is deemed non-natural automatically triggers a judicial inquiry.

Owono has made 47 international appearances for Equatorial Guinea.

The president of Equatorial Guinea's football federation, Venancio Tomas Micha, issued a statement on Tuesday offering "all our human and professional backing" to the player.

"As the involuntary protagonist of this tragic incident in the game, he is living through this situation with deep sorrow and distress," he added.

Jesus de Miguel joined Tenerife in 2025 on a three-year deal

On Tuesday, mourners laid flowers and lit candles beneath a black and white image of De Miguel at the Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez.

Tenerife said in a statement they will commence six official days of mourning, with all club activities suspended during this time.

The club's players, staff and officials will attend De Miguel's funeral, which will take place in Navahermosa, Toledo.

Tenerife will also open their home ground on Saturday evening to allow supporters to "bid a fitting farewell".

Tenerife and Andorra's Spanish second division matches scheduled for the weekend, against Granada and Mallorca respectively, have been postponed.

#1044. Why Man Utd's Roma comeback has echoes of Mourinho and Solskjaer

Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick (second left) hugs Shea Lacey after the 3-2 Champions League victory against Roma

It was impossible not to get swept up in the emotion and delirium of Manchester United's late 3-2 Champions League comeback win against Roma.

Old Trafford was transformed from a mutinous, baying cathedral of distrust and fury to one of joy and celebration.

Nine games and almost eight weeks is an eternity to wait for a victory at a club of Manchester United's size.

It didn't take Michael Carrick long to calm the mood.

"It's one win, so we're not getting too carried away with things, but it was an important win."

It was a huge result in the sense it bought Carrick some time. But given United's general state, no-one can be sure how much.

And, as was quickly pointed out in the aftermath of the victory, Manchester United have been here before.

Man Utd produce incredible second-half comeback to beat Roma

A half-time speech, a retaken penalty - and a win to save Carrick's job?

Jose Mourinho (centre) was sacked after a 3-1 defeat at Liverpool in December 2018

'Jose Mourinho set to be sacked whatever Manchester United's result vs Newcastle.'

As headlines go, it was attention grabbing.

As it turned out, the Mirror was wrong. Although United officials at the time tried to play down the situation, sources have since admitted the intention was to sack Mourinho after presiding over the club's worst start to a season in 29 years, and defeat by Newcastle would make it inevitable.

Much like the Roma game, the visitors raced into a two-goal lead and the atmosphere in the stadium started to turn, with most of the venom aimed at the director's box rather than the manager.

Mourinho, who had promoted Carrick to assistant coach, replaced Eric Bailly with Juan Mata after 19 minutes and it was Mata who scored the 70th-minute goal that sparked the comeback, completed by Alexis Sanchez in the final minute for a 3-2 victory.

After the game, Mourinho said the pressure on him was a "manhunt". However, the relationship between manager and club had been turning sour since the previous summer. His demand for Anthony Martial to be sold had been rejected, while record signing Paul Pogba was proving a problem.

While the Newcastle win sparked an improvement in form, a run of two wins in eight games culminating in a 3-1 loss at Liverpool led to Mourinho's dismissal 10 weeks later.

Former United defender Rio Ferdinand dismissed calls for Ole Gunnar Solskjaer to be sacked before the Champions League encounter with Atalanta on 20 October 2021 as representative of "current fan culture".

Carrick was also part of Solskjaer's coaching group as United went top of the Premier League when they beat Newcastle just over a month earlier, but two wins in seven suggested all was not well.

As he did with Roma, coach Gian Piero Gasperini saw his team establish a two-goal lead by half-time, then collapse. Cristiano Ronaldo was the matchwinner on this occasion, nine minutes from time for another 3-2 win.

Even if United had lost that night, it is hard to think Solskjaer's job would have been under threat. What followed immediately afterwards was a totally different story.

Liverpool came to Old Trafford and established a four-goal first-half lead. Jurgen Klopp's men won 5-0, their biggest ever away win over their old rivals.

Many United fans thought Solskjaer should go that night. It was three weeks later that it happened, after a 4-1 defeat at Watford.

Man Utd beat Roma - the other great Champions League comebacks

Fernandes critical of media 'lies' about Carrick relationship

Manchester United skipper Bruno Fernandes celebrates Matheus Cunha's winner against Roma

One look at the Premier League table shows why Carrick is right not to get carried away.

If results go against them, Manchester United could be bottom of the table by the time they kick-off against Aston Villa on Sunday.

Neither Mourinho nor Solskjaer could follow up their 3-2 successes with another victory. Mourinho's United drew at Chelsea, then lost at home to Juventus. Solskjaer's United were embarrassed by Liverpool. It meant neither man was able to build on the momentum generated by their epic victories.

United have gone seven Premier League games without a win. They went eight under Ruben Amorim at the end of the 2024-25 campaign, but draws and losses were split by victories en route to the Europa League final, so the effect was not as great as it feels right now.

The club does have an exceptional home record against Villa. They have won their past six in all competitions and lost just two league games against the Midlands outfit at Old Trafford since 1983.

When United sources finally communicated - almost 48 hours after the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth on 25 October - that Carrick and his players would be given the opportunity to turn the situation around, no timescale was put on this. However, the feeling was the forthcoming international break would be an appropriate time for the club hierarchy to take stock and decide what direction they should go in.

In the two games since, Carrick's team have been excellent across two halves.

Victory against Villa, albeit with Â£70m Carlos Baleba joining the injured list, would haul them up to within two points of Unai Emery's side heading into a tricky run of matches post international break, starting at Liverpool, but also including trips to Newcastle and Arsenal in December.

Defeat is likely to dump them in the relegation zone for at least a fortnight and facing severe baiting at Anfield on 22 November.

"It's not about me," is a phrase Carrick has repeated often as he has assessed the wreckage of another bad result. The outcome against Roma was much more positive.

There is no suggestion Carrick's future has been decided just yet. What happens at Old Trafford this weekend looks very important.

#1043. Rise of Germanic and Celtic languages is written in ancient DNA

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Aghascrebagh Ogham Stone in Northern Ireland shows much-worn inscriptions.Credit: Radharc Images/Alamy

More than one billion people worldwide speak Germanic languages such as English, German and Dutch, whereas Celtic languages — including Welsh, Irish and Gaelic — are spoken by only two or three million people, mostly in northern Europe.

A pair of studies analysing more than 4,700 ancient human genomes has now identified the possible origins of Celtic1 and Germanic2 languages and found migrations that might have dispersed their speakers around Europe — partly explaining their distribution today. The papers were published in Nature on 4 November.

Linguistic and archaeological studies have indicated that Celtic languages were widespread across Europe about 2,500 years ago, reaching into present-day Italy, Spain and France. Speakers of early Germanic languages might have been limited to a pocket of northern Germany, Scandinavia and the Baltic Sea coast some 3,000 years ago.

“We wanted to kind of see how this change occurs. How does the range swap through time?” says Hugh McColl, a population geneticist at the University of Copenhagen and a co-author of both studies.

How one language family took over the world: ancient DNA traces its spread

How one language family took over the world: ancient DNA traces its spread

Linguists have previously proposed that migrations played some part in the dispersal of Germanic and Celtic languages. But Guus Kroonen, a historical linguist at Leiden University in the Netherlands and a co-author of both studies, says that there are other ways for languages to spread. “You can easily adopt a new language without changing your genes.”

McColl, Kroonen and their colleagues looked for signs of migration through shifts in the ancestry of ancient population groups. To do so, they used newly sequenced genomes from more than 700 people, alongside published data from some 4,000 ancient humans.

The researchers identified an enigmatic population that migrated to Sweden around 4,000 years ago, possibly from Baltic regions. They found that the presence of this ancestry in Scandinavia and its spread throughout Europe was consistent with previous linguistic theories and archaeological evidence. “It’s a good tracer dye for the spread of Germanic languages,” says Kroonen.

For instance, the ancestry was present in southern Scandinavia and northern Germany around 3,000 years ago, when linguistic evidence points to exchanges with other language groups in this region. After some 1,000 years, the population moved into central, southern and western Europe, including the British Isles, which also chimes with linguists’ ideas and historical evidence about the spread of these languages, such as the first appearance of Germanic language inscriptions, called runes, around 2,000 years ago. The ancestry was present in Anglo-Saxon individuals in Britain, who spoke a Germanic precursor to Old English.

The study on the spread of Germanic languages also turned up a surprising ‘back-migration’ of people from present-day Germany into Scandinavia, which coincided with the emergence of Old Norse — the predecessor of modern Scandinavian languages — and with the Vikings’ influence on the region.

The Rök Stone, which bears the longest runic carving on stone with more than 700 characters, is thought to have been erected by Vikings in present-day Östergötland, Sweden.Credit: JEPPE GUSTAFSSON/TT News Agency/AFP via Getty

In many cases, the expansion of Germanic languages occurred in regions where Celtic languages were dominant.

Linguists debate both where Celtic languages emerged and how they became so widespread, says McColl, with some favouring an Atlantic origin overlapping with the current range of Celtic speakers in the British Isles. Other models put Celtic origins farther east, in Europe.

#1042. Why Chinese tech brands are outpacing Western rivals from EVs to robot vacuums

Do you remember the days when GoPro was synonymous with action cameras?

At its peak in 2015, the US company reigned supreme with around 6.6 million units sold that year and a market share of over 70%. Today, the pioneer is fighting for survival.

GoPro's biggest rivals, DJI and Insta360, entered the action camera market in 2019 and 2021, respectively. Today, they account for more than 90% of global smart handheld camera sales.

Alexander Hannemann, who regularly uses action cameras to film his motorcycle rides, says he switched from GoPro to Insta360 around two years ago.

"The quality is much better than a GoPro, even when I'm speeding up and going into corners at like 80 kilometers per hour," he told DW.

GoPro's case is not an exception. Since around 2010, many Chinese brands have not only caught up but surpassed once-dominant Western rivals across the consumer technology industry, from smart TVs to robot vacuums.

Gone are the days when "Made in China" stood for cheap, mass-produced products.

"China is still making affordable products today," says Chris Pereira, a Canadian entrepreneur and author with over 20 years of experience in China. "But the products are also high quality."

This combination has led to well over half of new consumer tech products globally coming from Chinese suppliers, Pereira adds.

BYD, Xpeng and other Chinese car manufactures sold almost two-thirds of all electric cars last year, surpassing incumbents like Tesla. In robot vacuums, Chinese brands dominate the global market, leaving former pioneer US company iRobot struggling to compete.

So why do Chinese companies increasingly outperform their Western rivals?

Pereira, whose consultancy iMpact helps Chinese companies gain traction overseas, attributes China's success to fierce domestic competition in cities like Shenzhen, Hangzhou and Shanghai; highly integrated supply chains and a can-do business culture that allows companies to innovate; and respond to problems quickly.

Other key reasons for China's competitive edge include unparalleled industrial automation, the strategic use of AI in manufacturing, responsiveness from regulators as well as relatively cheap labor, which together leads to significantly lower production costs and much faster innovation cycles than in the world's most advanced economies.

Joey Cheng, who moved to the US for his PhD studies over 20 years ago, is familiar with both the American consumer and the Chinese producer sides.

While his startup is based in the US, almost all the manufacturing is done in Shenzhen, where a large share of the world's hardware and consumer electronics are made.

"The supply chain in Shenzhen is basically inevitable for cost cutting and quick product development," Cheng says. "Especially as a startup you must get the product out quickly, or you'll get blown out of the water."

Although consumers are flocking to Chinese companies, some reservations persist.

A recent poll found that more than 90% of Europeans do not trust Chinese technology companies with their data, while about 80% distrust US firms. Germans expressed the highest level of mistrust.

Nadine, a German travel blogger who uses DJI and Insta360 products, says she wouldn't use any Asian products at home.

"My home robot vacuum is from a German company for precisely this reason: So the data remains compliant with German regulations. After all, manufacturers can connect directly to the camera," she said, referring to camera and audio hacking incidents involving robot vacuums.

Still, Pereira says that Chinese companies expanding abroad have to pay a "trust premium."

"This trust deficit means that they need to be extra competitive in terms of product and price in order for the market to choose them," he says, adding that the gap can be narrowed by a presence in overseas markets like BYD's first European passenger-car plant, expected to open in Hungary later this year.

Chinese companies say they comply with EU data protection rules. However, domestic security laws in the US and China can require firms to hand over data to authorities, and German officials note limited oversight of whether data is transferred from European servers abroad.

In light of security concerns, trade deficits and China's overall dominance, the US and several other Western countries have hit Chinese imports and companies with tariffs, blacklists and strict requirements. In late July, the Trump administration banned the import of humanoid robots manufactured outside the US.

A representative of Chinese robot maker Primebot told DW that all Chinese consumer tech companies are feeling the effects.

"We might seek cooperation with a local US company. Another potential solution is building a factory there," he said.

European countries and the EU are also weighing more tariffs against Chinese companies.

Chris Pereira foresees that the tariffs will accelerate two trends among Chinese companies: Moving more manufacturing overseas and an increasing focus on challenging top-tier Western brands with premium goods.

"Chinese officials and companies recognize that manufacturing needs to be localized to a certain degree. One reason is to assuage the challenges of exporting, another is to create trust locally," Pereira sums up.

"The other trend is that once duties wipe out the price advantage at the bottom, the margin left is at the top, so Chinese brands are increasingly competing directly with established Western names, where trust matters most."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

As China's dominance keeps growing, Western companies are scrambling to find ways to stay competitive.

Kaz Merchant, who works for a UK-based company that imports and exports IT hardware, says smaller companies, in particular, must carve out a geographic niche.

"They need to have their own unique selling point for a certain product, which China might not have for that region. Or they need to partner with a Chinese company," he says.

To Pereira, a key issue Europe needs to solve is regulators' responsiveness.

"Chinese regulators tell you very clearly and quickly what you can do. That speed helps companies iterate and succeed overseas," Pereira says.

"If you're waiting weeks for a response, you're going to lose business."

#1041. Who has made Troy's Premier League team of the week?

After every round of Premier League matches this season, BBC football pundit Troy Deeney will give you his team and manager of the week.

Here are this week's choices. Do you agree? Give us your thoughts using the comments form at the bottom of this page.

Bart Verbruggen (Brighton): He was unreal. Lots of saves which kept Brighton in it at Manchester City, even the last-ditch stop where it hit him in the face.

Just an impenetrable wall. Brighton should really have lost by two or three goals, but Verbruggen was the reason they managed to hold on for a 1-0 win.

Archie Gray (Tottenham): I'm going with a fully north London back four. Gray scored and defended really well against Crystal Palace. He was under a lot of pressure when Tottenham were in bad form and got a lot of stick, but now Spurs are starting to pick up I'm going to give him a bit of credit.

Ezri Konsa (Arsenal): He was a beast in Arsenal's 1-0 win at Anfield. Head it, kick it, throw your body in front of the ball. He defended and fought for the team, getting the job done.

Jan Paul van Hecke (Tottenham): Van Hecke got a goal and he's really growing into his role at Spurs. I still think he was a little bit overpriced, but all in all he's had a solid start, coming up with a few goals. Micky van de Ven next to him gives him confidence that he can go and be really aggressive, because Van der Ven will cover him with his pace.

Jurrien Timber (Arsenal): Timber got away with a shirt pull on Alexander Isak and I'm really surprised the referee and video assistant referee (VAR) didn't look at it. But I thought he recovered and defended really well at full-back.

Romeo Lavia (Chelsea): I thought Lavia was excellent for Chelsea. People will turn to Manchester United having 10 men, but the 60 minutes before that Chelsea were all over the place. Lavia was the only constant breaking up play, keeping the ball moving. Plus he had an assist.

Declan Rice (Arsenal): A proper captain's performance, he gets the job done all over the pitch. He got a little assist for himself, too.

Tatsuhiro Sakamoto (Coventry): Sakamoto goes unnoticed by a lot of people, but I think he works really hard for the team and he is very humble in his approach. On Saturday he also delivered in a massive win for his team against Sunderland.

Johan Manzambi (Aston Villa): Another assist for the 21-year-old who is just flying. His confidence is through the roof and he is taking over this Villa team. Really good player, only going to get better. He was taken off thinking about the Champions League game against Barcelona, but up until that point Fulham couldn't really stop him.

Ollie McBurnie (Hull): Grafter, scrappy, endeavour, goals, assists... he had it all in his game in the draw against Ipswich.

He epitomises what Hull are: a player that's always overlooked, a team that's always overlooked, but they've got some spirit and some fight.

Taiwo Awoniyi (Coventry): Unbelievable solo goal. It's really good to see the big fella back playing and being in a situation where he can impose himself. If Coventry are to stay up, he's going to be why.

Frank Lampard (Coventry): He has been really good. Coventry have taken care of business against Sunderland, it was a massive six-pointer and his team came out front-footed, aggressive and also did a job on a very good Sunderland team.

Also a massive nod to Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta for getting the job done at Liverpool.

Arsenal are looking to make January business - and one Hull player could be on the radar

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Arsenal have been linked with a breakout star of Hull City's good start to the season.

Well plenty expected the Tigers to be rooted to the bottom of the table following a play-off win at Wembley over the summer, Sergej Jakirovic's men have thus far bucked expectations to find themselves midtable, having lost just twice in their opening nine games.

With Premier League champions Arsenal hosting Hull this weekend, too, North London eyes may well be on one of the stars of the Yorkshire club.

Arsenal are back at the top of the table after a win at Anfield over the weekend saw the Gunners climb to the summit for the first time since winning the league last term – but there have been stutters already this season, as they look to conquer on all fronts once again.

Manager Mikel Arteta is apparently already identifying targets in forward areas, according to The Mirror, with dramatic defeats to the likes of Brighton & Hove Albion and Fleetwood Town in the League Cup highlighting the lack of depth that the Basque boss seemingly has in attack.

One potential option is Mohamed Belloumi, according to a new report from Maghreb Foot, via Sport Witness.

The winger has been a revelation in the top flight this season, leading the scoring charts for his club and making his international debut for Algeria this season, scoring two goals in his first three caps for the Fennecs.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Sport Witness relays that Beloumi “couldn’t refuse an offer” from Arsenal, who are now linked with a move for the star.

The 24-year-old certainly fits the profile of an Arteta attacker with excellent work ethic, while his ability to play on both flanks if necessary makes him a potential option for cover.

Arsenal already have the likes of Bukayo Saka, Noni Madueke and 16-year-old Max Dowman to play on the right wing – but with Madueke able to play on the left, Belloumi could be an option to become Saka's deputy, should Arsenal see him as better on that side.

FourFourTwo understands that Arsenal have their eye on a number of attackers who could strengthen their side either in January or next summer.

RB Leipzig star Antonio Nusa is one particular left-winger who has been linked with the Gunners in recent weeks.

Belloumi is worth €18 million, according to Transfermarkt. Arsenal travel to Slavia Prague this week as Champions League action continues this week.
